title: Revenge of the White Working Class
excerpt: L ast night, in the streets of Austin, Democrats honked their horns and hung out their windows, like it was V-E Day
body: L ast night, in the streets of Austin, Democrats honked their horns and hung out their windows, like it was V-E Day
In the nation’s capital, they blasted “Party in the U.S.A.” near the White House
But in southeast Iowa, the blue revolution came quietly

The Democrats of Des Moines County—a place that does not actually contain the state capital, but a small, industrial river city and rural areas along the Mississippi—have not come to associate Election Night with joy
The half dozen white-haired Iowans at the Burlington office’s “watch party” were blinking in disbelief at the TV as MS NOW election alerts flashed across the screen
Their party had retaken the governorship of Ohio—and somehow won a Senate seat in South Carolina? Texas was within reach

So, it seemed, was Kansas? “This might be a very big night,” Tom Courtney, a 79-year-old former state senator and former leader of the county party, told me, in what was already sounding like a colossal understatement
He and the other Democrats in the room seemed to be experiencing happiness only distantly, like birdsong from deep within a dark wood
This county, which had elected Barack Obama by about 23 points in 2008, was one of 31 Iowa counties that swung to Donald Trump in 2016
Two years ago, Trump won Des Moines County by 15 points, and Democrats began speaking of the “river counties” in the past tense—pieces of Iowa’s blue wall, lost forever
He paced the office, passing lawn signs, a cooling pot of chili, and the final slices of a Casey’s taco pizza
The countywide results were in, and a map of election results showed Des Moines County faintly—yet undeniably—blue
The county’s voters had opted to send a Democrat to the state house and another to the U.S
House; they’d also voted to make Rob Sand the state’s first Democratic governor elected in 20 years. “Did you hear that?” Courtney asked me, from across the room
By the end of the night, Iowa would also send Josh Turek to the Senate, plus three Democrats to the House
Kansas would send a Democrat to the Senate for the first time since the invention of beer in a can
In Ohio, the party would send Sherrod Brown back to Congress, and Amy Acton to the governor’s mansion

At the office in Des Moines County, Courtney’s wife, Nancy, emerged from the office kitchen with several plastic cups full of room-temperature peppermint schnapps. “We did good,” she told the small group of people, which, despite the cavalcade of thrilling news, was maintaining a measured, midwestern composure
A fortunate combination of variables had put Iowa, and the rest of the Midwest, back on the map for Democrats
The next big challenge for the party will be keeping it there
It’s all I heard at the polls yesterday morning in Iowa, where, like pretty much everywhere else, the midterm elections were a referendum on choices made by President Trump

Even loyal Republicans I spoke with at the polls seemed bummed to be voting for the GOP. “Somebody’s gotta do it,” one man told me outside Burlington’s First Church of Nazarene when I asked how he felt about Republican leadership
Later, a woman on the other side of town told me she was eating mostly toast and tacos to save money

She’d still submitted an all-Republican ticket, she said. “But I didn’t want to vote for any of them.” Still, to have a night like last night, Democrats needed more than bad atmospheric conditions for Republicans: They needed good candidates
And where it mattered most, they had them

In Iowa, Democrats ran Sand, a centrist who has emphasized frugality and promised to take on corruption. “Right person, right message, right place, right time,” Sandy Dockendorff, a longtime Democratic activist in Des Moines County, told me
Her party also had Turek, a four-time U.S
Paralympian whose compelling backstory and commitment to moderation proved enough to defeat Ashley Hinson, widely considered to be the star Republican recruit of the cycle
In Ohio, Sherrod Brown defeated Jon Husted, despite the latter’s allegedly fantastic posterior
And in Kansas, Democrats managed to get Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor who until recently was a Republican, at the top of the slate

It helped that Hamilton’s opponent, the incumbent Senator Roger Marshall, was impressively weak. “In a shitty environment, one way you don’t win races is to combine shitty candidates running shitty campaigns,” a senior—and very bitter—GOP strategist involved in multiple Senate races, said. [ Read: Who thought this ad was a good idea? ] The lesson, according to national Democrats, is clear: The winning candidates were “comfortable being a different type of Democrat,” the party strategist Lis Smith told me in a text

Those candidates had worked hard to persuade independents and Republicans, even if “it didn’t always earn them fans online.” Perhaps Smith is referring, in part, to the way that Sand and Turek handled some of the most contentious issues facing the party
Both candidates, for example, ditched the party line to say that transgender girls should not play in girls sports
Last week, Turek released an ad about it that had sent many Democrats sputtering

He won anyway. “Democrats need to get better at winning rural voters,” Adam Jentleson, president of the center-left think tank Searchlight Institute, told me. “Iowa is the testing ground, and Sand and Turek are the models.” [ Read: The simple message that produced a Democratic landslide ] Last night, every county in both Kansas and Iowa moved left

Dockendorff, the longtime Des Moines County activist, had told me over coffee yesterday morning that something like this would happen. (I trusted her because, in 2020, she had been the Cassandra of the caucuses, warning me —correctly—that Iowa’s vaunted nominating contest was likely to devolve into chaos.) “Iowa is turning back to purple,” she said
A year ago, or maybe less, Democratic activists had started filling chairs at county party meetings again
Energy wise, she said, “there is no comparison to 2018.” This was much, much bigger

River towns, like Burlington, where the decline of unions had hollowed out the party, were showing some potential for Democrats once more. “I hear dissatisfaction from voters here,” she said. “People trusted Trump to do
He hasn’t done .” This assessment inspired another warning from Dockendorff—for Democrats both in and outside of Iowa. “This is not a coronation of the Democratic Party,” she said

title: Google Won’t Give Schools the One Thing They Want
excerpt: Over the past few years, Google’s low-priced laptops have become an AI Trojan horse in America’s schools
body: Over the past few years, Google’s low-priced laptops have become an AI Trojan horse in America’s schools
Students can use a school-issued Chromebook to automate much of their homework
Fire up the Gemini app, and Google’s chatbot will spit out a full essay about the meaning of The Giver
Type an algebra question into the Google search box, and an “AI Overview” will solve it for you
Ask a follow-up question, and the search box might give way to “AI Mode,” which turns the search engine into a full-on chatbot
Districts across the country give each student their own device, which typically comes equipped with a Google account and a suite of the company’s software
Over the past year, some of the country’s largest public-school districts, including Los Angeles and New York City, have passed policies limiting students’ screen time and banning generative-AI tools
But they hit an obstacle: Google didn’t offer schools a way to fully opt out of AI
Yesterday, the tech giant’s attempt to address the problem only made people madder
Google’s stand-alone Gemini chatbot will now be disabled by default for school accounts, the company announced
But Google quietly left out any option to turn off its most popular and widely used generative-AI features: those built into its search engine
In other words, the only way for schools to go AI-free is to cut off students’ access to Google Search, the world’s most popular website

Tech companies threatening to withdraw products rather than modify them has become part of Silicon Valley’s playbook. (Meta once responded to a Canadian law requiring the company to share revenue with news publishers by banning news articles from its platform altogether.) Online, the move drew outrage, including from congressional Democrats who will soon hold newfound legislative and subpoena powers. “Google is once again prioritizing profits over people,” Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut posted . “Clearly, the Tech Giant is more concerned with forcing Gemini into schools than enabling students to succeed.” Google contended that the anger was based on a misunderstanding. “Today’s announcements give schools more choice, not less ,” the company posted on X, evincing a faith in the power of boldface font to get its message across
Google has never offered schools an AI-free version of its search engine (though there is a “Web” tab that limits results to links)
What was new in Google’s announcement was that both Gemini and Search will now be turned off by default, and schools will have the option to enable one or both

For schools that enable Search, the company is touting a new “guided learning” mode in its AI features that will prompt students to work through questions one step at a time, rather than simply giving them the answer

That could help address one of the biggest objections to Google’s AI search tools in the classroom, which is that they short-circuit the learning process. (A spokesperson for the company declined to comment beyond pointing me to its public statements.) [ Read: My son’s math homework is essentially just Pokémon ] Yet Google’s response to the blowback failed to address the aspect of its announcement that had upset people in the first place

The company wasn’t taking away any options that had existed before, but it also wasn’t providing the one option schools seemed to want most: a way to let students use Google Search without also enabling the AI bells and whistles
The unspoken logic behind the company’s stance is that, in some sense, all Search is AI search
AI Overviews and AI Mode launched in 2024 and 2025, respectively, but the company has been using large language models to help rank its search results since well before the arrival of ChatGPT
Google also used AI for years to help power the precursors to AI Overviews, including “featured snippets”—those bolded excerpts from web results that Google surfaced atop its list of links
So when Google says that opting out of AI entails opting out of Search, that’s technically true

Even so, there’s something obtuse about Google’s refusal to acknowledge that consumers—and schools especially—might reasonably draw a distinction between LLMs that help power search results and LLMs that generate answers themselves

Parents and teachers mostly don’t object to Google using AI to decide which webpages to link to when students ask a question (though there is a case to be made that the company’s opaque ranking process has always deserved more scrutiny than it’s received)
They object to turning Google into an instant-answer machine—and an error-prone one, at that
They object to students being conditioned to delegate their critical-thinking and source-evaluation skills to a machine
And they object to infusing the same site that indexes the world’s online information with a chatbot that can function as an ersatz friend or dispense personal advice to impressionable children
Which brings us to the business logic underlying Google’s stubborn stance
The company built its empire around a search tool that offered the shortest path between a user’s question and the information they were seeking
For years, that mostly meant refining its algorithm to downgrade spammy sites in its results
Then came ChatGPT, which promised to answer just about anything a user could ask, dispensing with the list of links altogether
OpenAI claimed this week that ChatGPT now handles about one-fifth as many search queries as Google
Chatbots are the most significant threat to Google’s core business that the search giant has ever faced
Its response has been to morph Search into an AI-answer tool in its own right
A few discontented users have dropped Google for niche alternatives such as DuckDuckGo, the privacy-focused search engine that now touts AI-free search as a selling point
Kamyl Bazbaz, a DuckDuckGo spokesperson, told me that usage of the company’s “No-AI” search option is up 30 percent since September
The company is now looking for ways to make it easier for schools that opt out of Google Search to switch their default search engine, he added
But Google seems to be betting that convenience will win out over qualms about generative AI
That bet could easily pay off, given how accustomed students already are to the tools Google has provided them with
While researching this story, I asked Google for data on how many Chromebooks are in U.S. schools

title: The Polls Found a New Way to Be Wrong
excerpt: Heading into the midterms, everyone who follows American politics had the same question: Were the polls correct, or would they underestimate Republicans once ag
body: Heading into the midterms, everyone who follows American politics had the same question: Were the polls correct, or would they underestimate Republicans once again? The answer turned out to be neither
This time around, the polls undercounted a different kind of voter: Democrats
According to the Silver Bulletin polling averages , Democrats were on track to win the U.S
House popular vote by nine points and narrowly flip a few Senate seats in states that Donald Trump had won by double digits
Democratic voters across the country saw these numbers and braced for disappointment
They remembered the polling misses of 2016 (which underestimated Trump by about three points on average) and 2024 (which did too) and believed that they could be watching another blue mirage
In fact, even this year’s seemingly incredible poll numbers turned out to significantly understate Democrats’ strength
Democrats are now expected to win the House popular vote by 13 points, the largest such victory in 50 years
And that four-point national polling error was small compared with the miss in certain states
In South Carolina, polls underestimated the Democratic candidate by five points on average; in Mississippi, by seven; in Texas, Georgia, and North Carolina, by nine
As a result, what was already expected to be a great night for Democrats turned into a rout of historic proportions
Americans used to reliably answer surveys
Now simply finding people willing to pick up the phone is an uphill battle
As response rates have declined, so has pollsters’ ability to reach a representative sample of the electorate
In 2016, pollsters underestimated Trump’s support among white voters without a college degree because they couldn’t poll enough of them
In 2020, the industry made a concerted effort to reach more of those voters
And yet the polls underestimated Trump by even more
Pollsters reasoned that even if they were now reaching the right educational groups, they must be missing certain personality types that were disproportionately likely to prefer Trump
Ahead of 2024, pollsters made a point of ensuring that their samples included enough 2020 Trump voters
That didn’t do the trick either—they managed to underestimate Trump yet again
This cycle, pollsters introduced even more bespoke solutions

In their jointly run polls, The New York Times and Siena College devised ways to discount respondents they deemed unrepresentative—rural white college-town residents, for example, might not be like other rural white voters—and started weighting respondents based on how Republican their name sounds or what car they drive
YouGov put resources into making sure that it had enough voters from not just purple neighborhoods but deep-red ones too

It also introduced new ways to model turnout, differentiating between a “strict” definition of likely voters and a “loose” one, because “strict” likely voters might include only the most engaged ones, and not the hard-to-reach ones who disproportionately support Trump and might still vote. [ Idrees Kahloon: Why Republicans lost so big ] Pollsters are scientists, but they are also humans
They do their best to avoid biases, and yet they have them anyway
The adjustments they made this cycle were in service of maximizing the accuracy of their surveys, yes, but they also had another goal: not getting burned again
The changes were unsubtly aimed at not overrating the Democrats’ chances
If pollsters had used these new techniques in 2024, they would have more closely predicted the final result
Nate Cohn, the chief political analyst for The New York Times , wrote over the weekend that the paper’s post-2024 weighting techniques made its polls look better for Republicans
In the past two midterms, in 2018 and 2022, pollsters nailed the final result with little systematic error
That’s probably because the voters that are hardest for pollsters to reach tend not to show up to vote in midterm elections, when the president isn’t on the ballot
By working hard to correct what went wrong in 2024, pollsters were solving for challenges that were less likely to come up this year anyway
Even so, in one sense, pollsters accomplished their goal: They were not burned by hidden Trump voters
Instead, the polls moved in the opposite direction, especially when it came to some minority groups

Tracking how different groups voted so soon after an election is difficult, but according to a sophisticated new model deployed this year by the Times , Hispanic voters in Texas swung toward Democrats by 42 points—10 more points than the polls predicted
Black voters’ nationwide support for Democrats was underrated by a similar amount
According to the polls, Democrats were set to win young men in battleground states by nine points after losing them badly in 2024
In the end, Democrats seem to have won that demographic nationwide by 24 points
In the long history of electoral polling, errors have not tended to favor one party over the other
That they no longer do is perhaps one more sign that the Trump era is ending.

title: Democrats Will Likely Disappoint Voters Soon
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
Democrats were jubilant last night, and for good reason: Few midterms in modern American history have produced such a thorough repudiation of a party as the Republicans experienced in this election
But celebrations have a pesky way of being followed by hangovers
For Democrats, the cause of their morning-after headache is affordability
Across the country, Democratic candidates campaigned and won by railing against Donald Trump’s handling of the economy
When they take control of Congress in January, however, they’ll find themselves with few direct levers to bring down prices
We don’t need to guess what happens to politicians who campaign on affordability and don’t deliver
Democrats can hardly be blamed for placing affordability concerns at the center of their campaign, alongside discussion of rampant corruption
This was good electoral politics—you want to run against your opponents’ weakness—and also good republican politics: It’s healthy for candidates to respond to voters’ concerns
The price of orange juice is up nearly 25 percent since Trump returned to office
The price of the candy that trick-or-treaters received on Halloween has risen 71 percent in five years
The average national price of a gallon of gas was more than $4 on Election Day for the first time in history
These price increases are a drag on many Americans’ budgets
Real wages—the difference between nominal wage growth and inflation—have declined over the past year, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics numbers released this week
For the Democrats, this has been a perverse political godsend
Long the undisputed party of workers, the Democratic Party has recently developed a reputation among voters for caring more about elites and cultural issues than basic economics
Trump demonstrated the power of focusing on inflation in 2024, when he assailed President Biden and Vice President Harris over rising prices

Trump never demonstrated any sort of plan for how he’d bring prices down, but his emphasis on the matter—along with Democrats’ muddled messaging about it—helped him overcome voters’ deep hesitations about his character
Since taking office, though, his lack of any vision for whipping inflation has been obvious
He has not pursued policies to fight high costs
He has demanded, in vain, that the Federal Reserve lower interest rates, which would be inflationary

He has mocked and dismissed the concept of affordability as a “hoax.” And although presidents typically have very limited short-term power to affect an economy, he found a way to make inflation worse by launching an ill-advised war in Iran, which he now has no idea how to end
This made Republicans very vulnerable in the midterms
But even with impressive wins in both the Senate and the House, Democrats will have few ways to bring prices down
On corruption, by some measures the top issue in the election , Democrats have room to hold Trump and his administration accountable using investigative powers
But on affordability, rhetoric and doomed bills designed to send a message are almost all they can offer
If reliable methods of bringing prices down in the short term existed, Republicans in Congress would have tried them this year
With unified Democratic control, Congress will be able to pass legislation, but Trump has already vowed to become “Mr

Veto.” Democrats can and will attempt to pressure Trump to end the conflict with Iran, but as the United States has seen repeatedly this century, starting a war is a lot easier than getting out of one. “People are impatient
They’re economically insecure,” Gina Raimondo told me in an interview last week

Raimondo, the commerce secretary under Biden, is often mentioned as a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate. “If we’re sitting here in a year and a half and we haven’t done a damn thing about cost and prices, people might say, Well, forget about you; I’m going to try the other guy .” Any parallel with voter rejection of Trump is imperfect

A president tends to shoulder more blame from voters than Congress does, a dynamic that is likely to be exacerbated with Trump, who is compelled to dominate attention, although it is sometimes to his disadvantage
But even if voters don’t blame Democrats specifically, they may still feel disillusioned with all politicians’ inability to bring quick change

That points to another risk for Democrats in 2028: not that people who voted blue in the midterms will turn against them, but that they will tune out entirely, just as the many disaffected Trump voters who opted not to vote in 2026 , rather than flipping to Democrats, did
The fact that party leaders are aware of these challenges doesn’t give them any easier answers to the affordability conundrum
Democrats had no choice but to campaign on high costs, but they may still pay a price for it

title: It’s the Morality, Stupid
excerpt: Last month, in Minneapolis, I visited the homegrown memorials that still stand in the spots where Alex Pretti and Renee Good were killed by federal agents
body: Last month, in Minneapolis, I visited the homegrown memorials that still stand in the spots where Alex Pretti and Renee Good were killed by federal agents

To me, they looked like living organisms fed by pain and hopefulness—handfuls of teddy bears with matted fur, crayon drawings of the victims, fresh daisies, tall red candles, cloth banners bearing expressions such as Only Love
Yesterday, on Election Day, these shrines were refreshed—this time by I voted stickers
The symbolism of these new offerings spoke succinctly to what the election seems to have meant to many voters
This was a chance for vindication, a response not just to Donald Trump’s policies but to the harsh and forbidding worldview he has come to represent
Pretti and Good were killed while monitoring an aggressive, armed, and often indiscriminate crackdown on their immigrant neighbors
Last night, more than 1,000 miles away from those memorials, in Austin, Texas, most of the people gathered for a victory speech by Senator-Elect James Talarico held signs that read Love Thy Neighbor

You might chalk these placards up to Talarico’s lefty Christian point of view, but they also felt like a modest plea, not the kind of thing you’d hold on a triumphant night: the expression of a desire for politics that spoke of simple values or, as Talarico himself put it, “love.” The election was about many things, and the polling clearly showed that economic pain topped the list, intertwined with concern about corruption

But alongside it ran a mushier motivation for the blue wave (or tsunami or earthquake or volcano; the metaphors in last night’s newscasts were as tired as they were plentiful) that impressed itself even on David Axelrod, the famously brass-tacks Democratic strategist. “We’ve been in a season of such cynicism and such anger,” he said as midnight neared and the results became definitive

Sounding more like a preacher than a pundit, he said the strong Democratic showing was evidence of our “common humanity.” People want, Axelrod said, “a season of decency.” Even some on the right could recognize, as Ben Shapiro did, a change in the “gestalt,” as he put it
To channel James Carville , it all felt like the genesis of a new truism about politics: It’s the morality, stupid
You don’t have to believe that Democrats’ hearts are somehow purer for making arguments premised on civility, or for promoting candidates who campaigned on restoring decency

Whether it was a premeditated effort or simply an instinctive collective response to 10 years of Trump, this kinder, more humane approach to political messaging was also a smart strategy. [ Read: Minnesota had its Birmingham moment ] In fairness, Democrats had some pretty good moral foils
Talarico’s rival, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, was impeached by Republicans over bribery and corruption, including pocketing a Montblanc pen

Ohio’s GOP candidate for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy, released an ad implying that his opponent was lying about being sexually abused as a child (and using her long-estranged mother, who had sided with the abuser, as a character witness)

Some of Ramaswamy’s party colleagues, including the outgoing governor, Mike DeWine, and former South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley , condemned the ad for having crossed a line (Haley went moral, calling Ramaswamy a “bad guy”)
But the most senior Republicans had no time for parsing the rightness of such an approach. “Stop whining,” J
Vance said to his fellow Republicans. “Whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern

What is my concern is who’s going to govern the next generation of American government.” ( His boss backed him up on this.) Judging from the astonishingly decisive results in Ohio and other red states, Americans of all kinds did have an opinion on its appropriateness, and voted accordingly

Chris Christie, the former New Jersey governor and onetime Trump ally, called the ad “an X-ray” of Ramaswamy’s “moral center.” He had harsh words, too, for Vance: “A man who wrote a book on Catholicism stood behind that ad
It’s a disgrace.” What Christie understood is something that Republican leaders, taking a cue from Trump, appeared to have forgotten
If politics seems too nakedly transactional, too much a game of power for power’s sake, it loses people
There might be a tribal aspect to how many Americans vote, but this identity has to be built around a story that feels righteous on some level
For a long time, Trump’s supporters could hear in his appeal an argument about justice, a case for the “forgotten man” to be remembered and rewarded
If he acted like a bully, he was their bully, for this virtuous purpose

But over the past two years, he has started a war that raised prices and put soldiers in danger, made Americans pay for tariffs, and spent much of his time gilding his immediate surroundings amid an affordability crisis
When the virtuous purpose vanishes, all that’s left is a bully
The wild shift in the Latino vote from 2024 might have resulted from the perception of this abandoned purpose
Trump lost nearly 30 points in this demographic compared with the last election; according to exit polls, 70 percent of Latino voters chose Democrats yesterday
The moral aspect of this shift could be seen in places such as Texas’s Rio Grande Valley
The region went Republican for the first time in modern history in the last election, largely because Latinos living near the border favored his promise to restore order there
Trump vowed to stop the flow of migrants into their neighborhoods and deport the criminals among them who were living in America
The crackdown, however, was far wider and crueler than many had anticipated, spreading fear throughout the entire area as ICE agents deported people who had been living in the country for decades
The local economy suffered, and those Latino voters felt not just betrayed by Trump but suddenly aware of an aspect of his approach that felt inhumane to them

Jessica Cantu Vuittenot, a former Trump supporter whose brother was detained just after he had checked in with an immigration official, described her regret to The New York Times : “Your world does go upside down because now it’s not just hurting you—it’s hurting your parents, it’s hurting his children, his grandchildren.” [ Read: Democrats are sounding more like Republicans ] Voters aren’t usually motivated by only one issue

Democrats’ focus on affordability, and on corruption in the Trump administration, surely helped turn so many districts blue, especially given the notable lack of focus from Trump himself in the closing weeks of the election
Surely in the mix, however, was a desire to recapture that sense of decency—a word many pundits tossed around after the results became clear

The move to run candidates such as Talarico—who might say, as he did last night with a straight face, that “every single person is holy”—helped provide a stark contrast, one that went beyond (or maybe, more accurately, underneath) differences in policy or ideology

This was not just the old question of a candidate’s character—of whether, for example, Adam Hamilton, the Kansan megachurch pastor, was a nicer person than his opponent, Roger Marshall, who had sued his patients over their medical debt
What Democrats offered was a way of speaking about American society that seems to have disappeared under Trump

title: Vance 2028 Is Here
excerpt: Vance’s strategy, since he became the Republican Party’s vice-presidential nominee in 2024, has been for President Trump to coronate him as his successor. “Dona
body: Vance’s strategy, since he became the Republican Party’s vice-presidential nominee in 2024, has been for President Trump to coronate him as his successor. “Donald Trump will ultimately decide who’s going to be the Republican nominee,” Vance told Sean Spicer last month, neatly excising the primary electorate from the decision matrix
Yet the midterm elections indicate the existence of a market among Republican voters for a 2028 presidential candidate who will distance their campaign from the current administration’s failures
Vance wants to be that Republican, but without forfeiting Trump’s support
How does he manage to do both? Blame everything on the Iran war
That is what Vance shrewdly, if disingenuously, has done

In a lengthy post on X , the vice president fully conceded that his party had been routed, and that “many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.” You often see analysts describing the 2024 Republican presidential electorate as “Trump voters,” but Vance understandably avoided this shorthand. [ Read: The simple message that produced a Democratic landslide ] He reduced the disaster to a single cause, writing: “The reason we lost is the war
The president himself said so last night.” This argument has several advantages
The Iran war has been a political debacle, both because it violated Trump’s oft-stated promise to avoid quagmires and because it drove up the cost of fuel and other goods
Second, and of equal importance, Trump likely agrees with this critique

The president has been publicly blaming Iran for months, while defensively insisting that the cost has been minor, temporary (the conflict has been two weeks away from ending since it began), and necessary to avoid nuclear cataclysm
In a Fox News interview last night, Trump insisted, “We actually have the greatest economy,” but “because of the gasoline price, people don’t see it as much as they would have without it

And the gasoline was caused by Iran.” Donald Trump Jr. quickly shared Vance’s post, commenting, “Every word of this is 💯💯💯,” stamping the royal family’s quasi-official imprimatur on Vance’s concession
Third, Vance’s argument aims to box out his most likely rival, Secretary of State Marco Rubio

If the war is the problem, then why would anybody prefer a Cabinet official whose entire job is foreign policy? Rubio is a well-known foreign-policy hawk, and blaming the hawks for snookering Trump into a mistake implicates the Rubio wing of the party for the midterm debacle
Fourth, Vance ignores every other way Trump dismantled the 2024 Republican coalition

Tariffs? Mass deportation? Corruption? The gilded-palace binge? A domestic agenda focused on cutting taxes for the rich, while throwing millions of low-income Americans off their health insurance and food stamps? Trump is not willing to cop to mistakes on any of them, and Vance either justified or enthusiastically supported all of these errors, anyway

In his X post, Vance specifically tried to refute Republican critics who (correctly) believe that the administration’s ironfisted approach to immigration enforcement alienated Latino voters who had expected a narrower approach focused on deporting criminals. “Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty,” Vance wrote. “I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance
But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you.” “Amnesty” is not the only alternative to Stephen Miller’s plan of deploying hastily trained masked agents and encouraging them to use the roughest tactics

But amnesty was a feature of an immigration-reform plan that Rubio briefly supported during Barack Obama’s second term, a historical fact that might explain Vance’s eagerness to revive the concept—as an epithet against his factional rivals

Vance’s post asserts that a pollster told him that disgruntled Trump voters—sorry, Trump/ Vance voters—would “come back on our team” if the administration did four things: 1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel

From a certain point of view that is especially prominent on the online right, those four things can be reduced to one thing: Trump has to stop letting Israel manipulate him into foreign wars, and instead focus on making Americans rich

Conveniently for Vance, Trump appears open to this critique, having blurted out on Fox News yesterday that he now favors phasing out American aid to Israel. [ David Frum: Things are going to get ugly ] Vance is right to imply that Israel helped persuade Trump to go to war with Iran
But Israel’s advocacy is not the only reason the Strait of Hormuz has been closed

Trump has argued on and off for attacking Iran since it emerged as an American bête noir during the hostage crisis that began in 1979, when Trump’s short list of immutable beliefs about the world first formed
Trump also seemed to drop his inhibitions about the use of military force after the kidnapping of Nicolás Maduro left him giddy with power

Blaming all of the administration’s domestic failures on the Iran war, while subtly pointing the finger at Benjamin Netanyahu for tricking the president into it, would seem to offer Vance the shortest and straightest path to holding together the MAGA coalition and his place within it
The Trump presidency is working perfectly well, and the only slight course correction required is to recommit to “America First” principles

Who among us might lead the MAGA movement into this new future of Trumpism-without-war? And without veering away from Trump’s militarized immigration strategy, or acknowledging the ongoing orgy of corruption and abuse of power? Only one man.

title: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
excerpt: Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts
body: Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts
But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position
Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton
Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott
At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years
Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail
Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing
At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September

That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities , began changing course himself.  Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails
On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits
Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether.  The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that
Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium
That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state
The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive

The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas

Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.  The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall
Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back
And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects
Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices
Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether

If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it

A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere.  It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas
Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton
Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift

But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red.  This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted

Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices.  Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state
And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns

So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.

title: What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?
excerpt: Divided government limits big federal moves: Democrats now control both chambers of Congress, but without a two-thirds majority, Trump has the power to veto leg
body: Divided government limits big federal moves: Democrats now control both chambers of Congress, but without a two-thirds majority, Trump has the power to veto legislation—dramatically narrowing what's actually possible over the next two years

State and local wins could matter more: Democrats flipped Pennsylvania's government and Georgia's utility regulator, signaling real potential for renewable energy progress at the local level, even as Washington could stay gridlocked

Voters turned sharply against data centers: Of 41 local ballot measures on data center development, nearly all look poised to end in more restrictions. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148022" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night

And it didn’t take long to see the beginning of the blue wave: Democrats took control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, a dramatic swing from Donald Trump’s victory two years ago.   While the results are striking, we probably won’t be seeing some of the big climate and energy policy shifts that have come in recent years as Congress and the presidency have changed hands
Instead, we’re entering a period of divided government, with a Congress that will likely do battle with Trump’s White House over the next two years

But even if the federal government isn’t likely to pass laws that overhaul energy and climate policy, the midterm results could be a big deal for energy, especially at the state and local level.  Let’s step back for just a moment to put these results in context
Readers might remember huge laws affecting climate and energy that were passed in just the last four years

The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act included massive support for clean energy, including tax credits and government grants and loans.Then the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act essentially slashed much of the support and financial incentives in the IRA from two years before

What those two laws had in common was a period when the government was entirely united, with the Senate, House of Representatives, and presidency all controlled by the same party—the Democrats in the first case and the Republicans in the second Now Democrats have captured a majority in both the Senate and the House
But Donald Trump is still in the White House
And crucially, neither chamber is anywhere close to a two-thirds Democratic majority
That’s the ratio that would be needed to override a presidential veto

So even if Congress puts together new legislation to boost climate measures and clean energy, Trump will need to sign it—and that dramatically narrows the scope of what might happen legislatively between now and the next election
There could be some bipartisan compromises
One interesting bit of legislation to watch immediately after the election is what happens with permitting reform
In late September, a bipartisan group of senators put forward a bill that would overhaul how new energy projects are reviewed and approved in the US
The law aims to cut red tape and speed up the permitting process
The Senate is set to vote on that package, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, on November 9, before the new Congress takes control in January
The White House has supported the bill, and it could pass the Senate if just a handful of Democrats join the Republican majority
But now, we might see Democrats wait until next year to try to renegotiate a deal, though anything would still need to pass muster with Trump
With Democratic control of Congress, we’ll likely see much more scrutiny of Trump and agencies controlled by his appointees
Democratic leaders have already signaled plans to go after leaders like EPA commissioner Lee Zeldin over cuts to staff and investments
Democrats will have the power to subpoena cabinet members and open investigations
Looking beyond the national results, a major trend to watch moving forward will be local action
Democrats swept local control of Pennsylvania, and officials there have signaled plans to support renewable energy and efforts to cut greenhouse-gas emissions
Democrats also took control of the Georgia Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years
The group regulates electric utilities, essentially controlling much of the grid’s buildout
Among the broadest effects of these election results, though, will be for the data center industry
According to tracking from Ballotpedia, there were 41 local ballot questions related to data centers
And overwhelmingly, voters chose to restrict their development
Nearly every single one of these measures looks set to come down against data center development, as of the morning of November 4
And AI critics fared well in their races, too
Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governor’s seat in Texas, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott

During her campaign, Hinojosa called for a law to completely pause data center development; if passed, it could have major implications for both the state’s grid and the data center industry more broadly
We might not see dramatic new climate- or energy-related federal legislation between now and the next major US election
But many voters signaled, and quite loudly, that they wanted a change
We’ll see how much will shift in the next two years, and where that leaves us.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter

title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
excerpt: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communication
body: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes
The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep

When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents
DOWNLOAD THE REPORT This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically

As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms
In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem
Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient
Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves
Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows

title: I study polling failures – this time, pollsters were mostly right, if not precise
url:
<title>I study polling failures – this time, pollsters were mostly right, if not precise</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770099/original/file-20261104-78-8j37jk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8640%2C5760&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Voters cast their ballots at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine in New York on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Election2026AmericaVotesNewYork/f4656c5b36b548edbe49ea8823bc01e9/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=election%20midterms%20US&amp;currentItemNo=37&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The crucial test for preelection polls is whether they broadly indicate <a href="https://x.com/Mark_Penn/status/2117882684751884343">how voters are likely to decide</a>. By that fundamental measure, the 2026 midterm polls largely succeeded in anticipating outcomes on Election Day. </p>

<p>If somewhat tentatively, the polls overall had been <a href="https://nymag.com/intelligencer/article/pretty-much-every-poll-is-good-for-democrats-now.html">signaling important gains for Democrats</a>. And that is what voting produced.</p>

<p>It was, perhaps, polling’s most reassuring performance since <a href="https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/president/general/2008/mccain-vs-obama">accurately anticipating Barack Obama’s presidential election</a> in 2008, an outcome cited in my book, <a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/lost-in-a-gallup/paper">“Lost in a Gallup: Polling Failure in U.S. Presidential Elections.”</a> </p>

<h2>Two truisms confirmed</h2>

<p>This is not to say the 2026 preelection polls offered precision estimates before returns poured in. They appear to have <a href="https://www.foxnews.com/politics/america-saw-blue-wave-coming-drastically-underestimated-extent-dem-tsunami">underestimated support for Democratic candidates</a> in some Senate races. </p>

<p>But spot-on precision, while enviable, is not what polls can be expected to produce, considering the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/2330443X.2021.1971126">many ways error can infiltrate</a> opinion surveys. Given their <a href="https://theconversation.com/no-cheery-time-for-election-pollsters-in-run-up-to-us-midterms-289772">checkered record in recent national elections</a>, pollsters and media analysts tended to couch their end-of-campaign assessments in <a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/2026/10/midterm-polls-error/688922/">measured tentativeness</a>.</p>

<p>For example, Nate Cohn, chief political analyst for The New York Times, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/upshot/poll-times-siena-senate-midterms.html">wrote just before the election</a> that “it’s reasonable to wonder whether the polls might be overestimating Democratic strength yet again. This is a real possibility. President Trump’s supporters are relatively unlikely to respond to polls, which introduces the ever-present risk of a polling misfire.”</p>

<p>That risk was mostly unrealized, as Republican candidates were swept in <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/democratic-midterms-wipeout.html?unlocked_article_code=1.N1E.ia0W.PPiKVVjajWqm&amp;smid=url">a red wipeout</a>.</p>

<p>The 2026 polls tended to confirm the truism in American politics that midterms typically are rough on <a href="https://spia.uga.edu/expert-voices/why-does-the-presidents-party-usually-lose-seats-in-midterm-elections/">candidates of the party that holds the presidency</a>. </p>

<p>Another truism, again reaffirmed, is that a president’s approval ratings often are <a href="https://www.wsj.com/livecoverage/midterm-election-news-2026/card/why-a-president-s-job-approval-rating-matters-L0iVimxfJYbbaYmFCB9O">useful in gauging</a> the country’s mood before midterm elections. President Donald Trump’s preelection approval ratings <a href="https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/approval/donald-trump/approval-rating">hovered at or below 40%</a>, according to survey data compiled by RealClearPolitics.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770124/original/file-20261104-64-kms92m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Several people hunch over voting booths inside a hall." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770124/original/file-20261104-64-kms92m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770124/original/file-20261104-64-kms92m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770124/original/file-20261104-64-kms92m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770124/original/file-20261104-64-kms92m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770124/original/file-20261104-64-kms92m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770124/original/file-20261104-64-kms92m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770124/original/file-20261104-64-kms92m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Voters cast their ballots at the Bridge of Hope Church in Youngstown, Ohio, on Nov. 3, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/voters-cast-their-ballots-inside-a-polling-location-at-the-news-photo/2302878545?phrase=Election%20polls&amp;adppopup=true">Jeff Swensen/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The U.S. war with Iran, launched by Trump, was <a href="https://www.wsj.com/politics/elections/trump-acknowledges-iran-war-is-partly-to-blame-for-republican-losses-c3cf572e">a major factor propelling the unenviable ratings</a>. The conflict went unresolved while <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/data-graphics/gas-prices-iran-war-state-national-cost-trump-rcna265835">fuel prices surged</a>, bringing pain to consumers.</p>

<p>Those and other problems <a href="https://www.natesilver.net/p/its-judgment-day-for-trump-and-for">prompted polling analyst Nate Silver</a> to write that Trump “almost seems to have a death wish in these midterms. And the one superpower he has – turning out low-propensity voters in presidential years, the sorts of voters who apparently are often missed by pollsters – has never really worked when Trump himself wasn’t on the ballot.”</p>

<p>And it didn’t work this time, either, even though throughout the campaign Trump encouraged supporters to <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6055367-trump-midterm-republican-voters-pretend-ballot/">pretend his name was on the ballot</a> and turn out to vote.</p>

<h2>Few polling misses</h2>

<p>When examined closely, the polls delivered some disagreement in the days before the election. Pollsters offered ranges that, in some races, were sizable. </p>

<p>For example, was Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton <a href="https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/senate/general/2026/texas/talarico-vs-paxton?card=159113&amp;t=1793793732067">up by 1 percentage point</a> in Texas late in the campaign, or was he <a href="https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/senate/general/2026/texas/talarico-vs-paxton?card=159247&amp;t=1793793767324">down 7 points</a>? Paxton lost by double digits to Democrat James Talarico, a margin that no pollster anticipated.</p>

<p>Similarly, was long-serving Republican Sen. Susan Collins <a href="https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/senate/general/2026/collins-vs-jackson?card=159347&amp;t=1793794096175">ahead by 2 points</a> in Maine or was she <a href="https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/senate/general/2026/collins-vs-jackson?card=159379&amp;t=1793794123871">losing by 9 points</a>? The outcome was <a href="https://www.realclearpolitics.com/elections/live_results/2026/state/me/senate/">closer to the latter reading</a>, with Democrat Troy Jackson winning by more than six points. </p>

<p>In Minnesota, was Democratic Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan <a href="https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/senate/general/2026/minnesota/tafoya-vs-flanagan?card=158940&amp;t=1793794316003">up by 14 points</a>, or by <a href="https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/senate/general/2026/minnesota/tafoya-vs-flanagan?card=159365&amp;t=1793794357830">just 2 points</a>? With most votes counted by the day after the election, Flanagan’s margin of victory was <a href="https://www.realclearpolitics.com/elections/live_results/2026/state/mn/senate/">about 10 points</a>.</p>

<p>Such polling gaps in high-profile races offer a reminder to not focus on any single survey but, instead, to consider overall polling averages, which tend to remove or reduce the effects of outliers.  </p>

<p>None of this necessarily is to declare that pollsters have resolved their persistent <a href="https://aapor.org/polling-accuracy/">problems in sampling</a>, especially in interviewing hard-to-reach voters. But big polling misses <a href="https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/governor/general/2026/texas/abbott-vs-hinojosa">like that in the Texas governor’s race</a> – where Democrat Gina Hinojosa won by double digits, although polls had shown Republican Gov. Greg Abbott ahead by a few points – were few this election cycle.</p>

<p>Meanwhile, the electorate’s broad inclinations were plainly if not precisely depicted.</p>

<p>That outcome has to be heartening for pollsters, an often-<a href="https://thehill.com/opinion/campaign/5586880-2024-election-polling-accuracy/">beleaguered</a> and <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/30/poll-americans-dont-trust-polls-01141115">much-criticized</a> cohort.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295433/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Florida just voted for lower property taxes – and that could mean cuts in government services and new housing construction</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770128/original/file-20261104-64-mt5ysk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5478%2C3652&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Over 60% of Floridian voters voted to cut property taxes, which has been surging in recent years.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Election%202026%20America%20Votes%20Florida/0f73e585eb744888b0e0e58f79d95823/photo">AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell)</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Many Florida homeowners cheered on Nov. 3, 2026, when more than 60% of voters <a href="https://baynews9.com/fl/tampa/news/2026/11/04/florida-voters-approve-amendment--providing-property-tax-relief-for-homeowners">approved a constitutional amendment</a> to significantly reduce property taxes.</p>

<p><a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Florida_Amendment_3,_Homestead_Tax_Exemptions,_Property_Assessments,_and_Spending_Restrictions_Amendment_(2026)">Under the measure, Amendment 3,</a> a homeowner’s tax break, known as a <a href="https://ocpaweb.ocpafl.org/faqcontent/HX_FAQ">homestead exemption</a>, would triple from the current US$50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and increase again to $250,000 in 2028. By shielding more of a home’s assessed value from taxation, this exemption effectively lowers homeowners’ tax bills. New homeowners <a href="https://floridaphoenix.com/2026/07/07/another-amendment-3-challenge-filed-by-bipartisan-pair-of-former-legislators/">would also reportedly be eligible</a> for a property tax break, but on a more phased-in basis. </p>

<p>But the measure comes with a hefty price tag. The Florida Legislature’s research arm <a href="https://edr.state.fl.us/Content/about/index.cfm">estimated the measure</a> would reduce annual revenue from property taxes by <a href="https://edr.state.fl.us/Content/conferences/revenueimpact/archives/2026F/_pdf/impact0612.pdf">$11.8 billion</a>. This translates to a <a href="https://floridataxwatch.org/2023-how-florida-counties-compare/">30% reduction</a> in revenue for Florida counties and a 13% cut for smaller municipal governments.</p>

<p>While homeowners will get some relief, the budget crunch due to the lower tax revenue will affect other Floridians in more adverse ways. <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=sAMhsxQAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">As economists</a> <a href="https://www.ut.edu/directory/wood-aaron-d">who have been following</a> the debates over Amendment 3, we argue that local governments will struggle to fund basic services with less money. And we expect more sweeping economic consequences as well – including less affordable residential housing and a broader shift of the tax burden away from relatively wealthier homeowners to those who are less well off. </p>

<h2>How Amendment 3 would work</h2>

<p>Much of the political momentum for Amendment 3 came from a rise in the cost of living and <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/realestate/florida-property-tax-vote-midterms.html">frustration over rising property taxes</a>. These now average <a href="https://smartasset.com/taxes/florida-property-tax-calculator#O4NOGqPK5X">just over $3,000</a> annually but can run much higher for Floridians with <a href="https://smartasset.com/taxes/florida-property-tax-calculator">more expensive homes</a>. </p>

<p>In addition to raising the homestead tax exemption, Amendment 3 lowers the cap on annual assessments on rental and commercial properties from <a href="https://ocpaimages.ocpafl.org/api/Content/GetContentDynamicFile?contentFileID=149816">a 10% increase</a> to <a href="https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2026F/2F/BillText/c1/PDF">a 5% increase</a>. Since property taxes are based on an asset’s assessed value, this language effectively limits but doesn’t rule out tax hikes for businesses. </p>

<p>So landlords, for example, could still see <a href="https://www.flhouse.gov/Sections/Documents/loaddoc.aspx?BillNumber=1&amp;DocumentType=Analysis&amp;FileName=h0001z.SAC.DOCX&amp;Session=2026F">meaningful annual tax increases</a> as their properties go up in value – costs that would <a href="http://dx.doi.org/10.21799/frbp.wp.2025.41">likely be passed on</a> to renters. </p>

<p>Amendment 3 makes clear that school-related property taxes <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Florida_Amendment_3,_Homestead_Tax_Exemptions,_Property_Assessments,_and_Spending_Restrictions_Amendment_(2026)">are exempt</a> from these tax cuts. It also lists <a href="https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2026F/2F/BillText/c1/PDF">some theoretical limits</a> on how local governments should use tax dollars, as a way to ensure continued funding for essential services such as public safety, infrastructure or obligations for employee retirement benefits. </p>

<p>But it also states that funds may be used for “<a href="https://www.flhouse.gov/Sections/Documents/loaddoc.aspx?BillNumber=1&amp;DocumentType=Analysis&amp;FileName=h0001z.SAC.DOCX&amp;Session=2026F">expenditures approved</a>” by local and county governments – ambiguous wording that suggests these stipulations can be breached. </p>

<h2>Who pays the bill?</h2>

<p>Florida property taxes are levied and collected by some 640 local government entities. There’s <a href="https://floridarevenue.com/property/Documents/ptoinfographic.pdf">no state income tax</a>, so any reductions in property tax revenue directly affect local and county governments.</p>

<p>With tax revenue slashed, businesses, landlords and owners of other non-homestead properties like second homes would almost certainly see their taxes go up. This is a typical pattern: <a href="https://edr.state.fl.us/content/presentations/property-tax-study/EDR-Presentation-on-Interim-Findings.pdf">When governments</a> <a href="https://taxfoundation.org/research/all/state/property-tax-repeal-replace-revenue/">cut property taxes</a> for some groups, <a href="https://www.lincolninst.edu/publications/books/erosion-property-tax-base/">taxes shift</a> to other groups. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Fire department workers help with water rescues near Orlando, Fla., after Hurricane Milton, Oct. 10, 2024." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770130/original/file-20261104-64-r0xkba.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770130/original/file-20261104-64-r0xkba.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=347&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770130/original/file-20261104-64-r0xkba.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=347&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770130/original/file-20261104-64-r0xkba.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=347&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770130/original/file-20261104-64-r0xkba.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=437&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770130/original/file-20261104-64-r0xkba.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=437&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770130/original/file-20261104-64-r0xkba.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=437&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Essential public services, including fire and police departments, could face sharp budget cuts due to the shortfall from lower property taxes.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Hurricane%20Milton%20Weather/3f2648803b3a416e99b6517dbbd292be/photo">Orange County Fire Rescue Department via AP</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>This dynamic is likely to play out with local governments as they try to keep revenue stable: Amendment 3 would force them to <a href="https://edr.state.fl.us/Content/revenues/reports/fiscal-analysis-in-brief/FiscalAnalysisinBrief2025.pdf">hike taxes in other areas</a> to make up for the shortfall. This could include increases in state and local sales taxes, an expansion of the list of goods <a href="https://floridarevenue.com/forms_library/current/dr46nt.pdf">subject to sales taxes</a>, or a hike in “<a href="https://floridarevenue.com/Forms_library/current/gt800014.pdf">documentary stamp taxes</a>,” which are required on documents such as deeds, bonds and mortgages. </p>

<p>State and local governments could also impose higher fees for specific services, such as <a href="https://floridadep.gov/sites/default/files/2023%20Florida%20Solid%20Waste%20Disposal%20Fees.pdf">solid waste treatment</a> and <a href="https://fsa.memberclicks.net/stormwater-utility-rates-in-florida">stormwater utilities</a>. Another option is to hike <a href="https://hcfl.gov/businesses/permits-and-records/permit-fees">permits and inspection fees</a>, <a href="https://impactfees.org/florida-impact-fees">fuel taxes</a> or other <a href="https://floridalicenseplate.org/vehicle-registration-fees">service charges</a> such as vehicle registration fees. </p>

<p>Finally, local governments could raise <a href="https://floridarevenue.com/taxes/taxesfees/Pages/local_option.aspx">tourism-related taxes</a>, such as on food, beverages and hotels. But this recourse wouldn’t help counties with limited tourism, and such revenues fluctuate in any event.</p>

<p>In the end, though, essential services would still almost certainly be affected. Funding for police, fire and emergency medical services is <a href="https://edr.state.fl.us/Content/local-government/data/revenues-expenditures/stwidefiscal.cfm">primarily the responsibility</a> of local governments, and, for most counties, they make up the <a href="https://flicg.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/revenue-and-expenditure-booklet-2021_WEB-Version.pdf">largest line item</a> in their annual expenditures. Reducing <a href="https://edr.state.fl.us/Content/local-government/data/revenues-expenditures/stwidefiscal.cfm">property taxes</a> would amount to a direct hit, especially in smaller, less-populated counties. </p>

<p>And if local governments do raise sales tax rates to the extent they can, lower-income Floridians will bear a disproportionate burden as they spend much more of their income on consumption. They’re also far more likely to rent than own a home, so any increased rents would take a bigger toll.</p>

<h2>A looming affordable housing crunch?</h2>

<p>Less noticed in the debate over Amendment 3 was how it would affect the state’s <a href="https://www.jpmorgan.com/insights/real-estate/community-development-banking/floridas-affordable-housing-crisis">affordable housing shortage</a>. We argue that the structure of the property tax cut will likely create more incentives for counties and developers to build commercial structures instead of more residential housing.</p>

<p>When developers build residential homes, they require a basic level of public services to support residents and the local infrastructure. In fact, property taxes in much of Florida effectively subsidize residential home development: For every dollar that a homeowner pays in property taxes, <a href="https://hcfl.gov/government/your-property-tax-investment">it costs county governments around $1.20</a> to provide those services. This gap will only grow when property tax revenues fall.</p>

<p>From the standpoint of local and county governments, then, <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/local-taxation-land-use-regulation-and-land-use_52da7c6a-en.html">it may make more sense</a> to focus on commercial or industrial construction as a way to keep tax revenues stable. But <a href="https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/09/florida-homestead-exemption-proposal-could-reshape-family-development">with fewer homes built</a> at the expense of business construction – from manufacturing to data centers – the supply squeeze will only drive up prices and rents for the workers who are needed for those jobs. </p>

<p>Now that Amendment 3 is on the books, Florida’s county and local governments will confront major trade-offs. We believe that state officials will come to realize how much of a change has been made – and how quickly their priorities may have to shift.</p>
