<title>Why one positive E. coli sample put a Pittsburgh-area community under a boil-water advisory</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770111/original/file-20261104-64-k5zpx4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=4%2C0%2C2115%2C1410&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Boiling makes tap water safe during advisories.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/boiling-water-in-stainless-pan-in-kitchen-royalty-free-image/1324515862?phrase=pot%2Bof%2Bboiling%2Bwater">karimitsu/iStock via Getty Imags Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>A boil-water advisory was issued on Nov. 2, 2026, by officials in Center Township in Beaver County, 25 miles from Pittsburgh, after a routine sample tested positive for coliform bacteria, including <em>E. coli</em>, according to the <a href="https://www.ctwa.us/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/FINAL-NOTICE-COLIFORM-PUBLIC-NOTICE-FOR-TEXT-MY-GOV-11022026.pdf">township’s water authority</a>. </p>

<p>The advisory <a href="https://www.post-gazette.com/local/region/2026/11/03/boil-water-advisory-center-twp/stories/202611030032">stayed in place</a> while the authority kept testing, and Central Valley School District students stayed out of school buildings and <a href="https://www.parentsquare.com/feeds/95446017">attended class remotely</a> on Nov. 3-4 as a precaution. The authority lifted the advisory on Nov. 4.</p>

<p><iframe id="1KElF" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/1KElF/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Beaver County is in the far west of Pennsylvania"></iframe></p>

<p>A single positive sample of <em>E. coli</em> can upend daily routines for an entire community, from what people drink to how they wash dishes, and leave residents wondering how worried they should be. </p>

<p>Two environmental engineers, <a href="https://cee.engineering.cmu.edu/directory/bios/fakhreddine-sarah.html">Sarah Fakhreddine</a> and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=oh7m3vEAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">Marlee Shaffer</a>, explain why <em>E. coli</em> in <a href="https://theconversation.com/nearly-60-million-americans-dont-drink-their-tap-water-research-suggests-heres-why-thats-a-public-health-problem-158483">tap water</a> is a red flag, how boiling kills harmful germs, and how utilities decide the water is safe again.</p>

<h2>How does <em>E. coli</em> get into drinking water?</h2>

<p>When <em>E. coli</em> is detected in a drinking-water system, it means the water may contain harmful bacteria, viruses or parasites. Most strains of <em>E. coli</em> don’t make people sick, but <em>E. coli</em> is a common bacterium that <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/ecoli/about/index.html">lives in the digestive systems</a> of people and animals. That’s why scientists use it as an indicator: Its presence flags that water has been contaminated by human or animal waste, which can carry germs that do cause illness.</p>

<p>A drinking-water system <a href="https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/how-does-your-water-system-work-text-only">treats water so it is safe for people to drink</a> and delivers that clean water to customers’ taps. <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/drinking-water/causes/">Water can become contaminated</a> during treatment or delivery, as it moves through the system’s pipes.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770114/original/file-20261104-64-xvedvc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A lab technician tests a water sample." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770114/original/file-20261104-64-xvedvc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770114/original/file-20261104-64-xvedvc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770114/original/file-20261104-64-xvedvc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770114/original/file-20261104-64-xvedvc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770114/original/file-20261104-64-xvedvc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770114/original/file-20261104-64-xvedvc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770114/original/file-20261104-64-xvedvc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Utilities routinely test water samples to catch contamination before it reaches customers’ taps.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/lab-technician-adding-liquid-from-graduated-royalty-free-image/910264704?phrase=water%20sample%20testing&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Huntstock/DisabilityImages Collection via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>If there’s a problem with the treatment process, harmful pathogens may not be fully removed from the water. Or treatment may be working well, but a pipe breaks somewhere in the system and pressure drops. That can allow contaminated water to enter the pipes that deliver water to homes and businesses.</p>

<h2>Why can one positive sample trigger a boil-water advisory?</h2>

<p>The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency <a href="https://www.epa.gov/dwreginfo/revised-total-coliform-rule-and-total-coliform-rule">sets a goal of zero <em>E. coli</em></a> in drinking water. A single water sample is a snapshot of water quality at the time and place it was collected. Because drinking water systems are interconnected, with water flowing through them, a problem in one location might mean water elsewhere could also be contaminated. </p>

<p>How much of the system is affected depends on where and why the problem occurred. It can take time for a utility to find the problem, fix it and test more water samples. A <a href="https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/pda/documents/consumer_protection/foodsafety/documents/Emergency%20Guideline%20for%20Boil%20Water%20Notices%20in%20Retail%20Food%20Facilities.pdf">boil-water advisory</a> helps keep the public safe while the utility investigates and addresses the problem.</p>

<h2>What does boiling the water do?</h2>

<p>Boiling water kills harmful bacteria and protozoa and inactivates viruses that might be in the water. High temperatures damage key structural parts of these microorganisms, leaving them unable to multiply and cause infections. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-FWC-WSH-15.02">Research shows</a> that at the temperatures water reaches when it boils, most harmful microbes are killed in under a minute. It can also help to keep some bottled water on hand in case you are unable to boil water.</p>



<h2>How do water utilities determine when the water is safe?</h2>

<p>Water utilities must show the water is safe and get approval before lifting a boil-water advisory. They have to investigate what caused the <em>E. coli</em> contamination, fix the problem and then keep testing to make sure no more samples come back positive. They share this information with their state or federal regulatory agency, which decides whether the utility has met the requirements to lift the advisory. </p>

<p>In Pennsylvania, the state Department of Environmental Protection requires a utility to <a href="https://amwater.com/paaw/water-quality/what-is-a-boil-water-advisory">show two consecutive days of negative samples</a> after addressing the problem.</p>

<h2>Why can’t kids go to school during a boil-water advisory?</h2>

<p>In a school cafeteria, for example, an advisory affects not just drinking water but also the water used to wash fruits and vegetables, cook food and wash dishes. Meeting those requirements can be challenging, depending on the school’s size, its resources and whether it can get other sources of water, such as bottled water that has been transported in by truck. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770117/original/file-20261104-64-th9xoi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A young girl drinks bottled water." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770117/original/file-20261104-64-th9xoi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770117/original/file-20261104-64-th9xoi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=439&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770117/original/file-20261104-64-th9xoi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=439&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770117/original/file-20261104-64-th9xoi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=439&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770117/original/file-20261104-64-th9xoi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=552&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770117/original/file-20261104-64-th9xoi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=552&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770117/original/file-20261104-64-th9xoi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=552&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A boil-water advisory affects a school’s drinking water and also how its cafeteria cooks, cleans produce and washes dishes.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/year-old-alisa-regressa-a-second-grader-from-the-eliot-news-photo/1340359038?phrase=school%20cafeteria%20water&amp;adppopup=true">MediaNews Group/Boston Herald via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Some schools may be able to stay open and comply with the advisory, while others may decide to close or switch to virtual learning to ensure safety. Children can be <a href="https://www.epa.gov/children/water-contamination-and-young-children">more vulnerable than healthy adults to waterborne illnesses</a>, so compliance by schools is especially important.</p>

title: NASA’s Swift telescope has burned up, months after a robot sent to save it failed – here’s why it’s so hard to boost a satellite

<title>NASA’s Swift telescope has burned up, months after a robot sent to save it failed – here’s why it’s so hard to boost a satellite</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769911/original/file-20261104-64-ktbpnd.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=116%2C72%2C1511%2C1007&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory orbits above Earth in this illustration. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.nasa.gov/missions/swift/nasa-explores-industry-possibilities-to-raise-swift-missions-orbit/">NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center/Chris Smith (KBRwyle)</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory took its last <a href="https://theconversation.com/swifts-telescope-reveals-birth-deaths-and-collisions-of-stars-through-1-million-snapshots-in-uv-97044">look at the sky</a> on Oct. 20, 2026, while orbiting about <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/2026/10/23/nasas-swift-mission-ends-ahead-of-re-entry/">171 miles (275 kilometers)</a> above Earth. NASA ended the telescope’s mission three days later, because Swift had sunk so low that drag from the thin air there meant its telescopes couldn’t hold steady. The <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/2026/11/02/nasas-swift-observatory-to-re-enter-atmosphere/">telescope reentered the atmosphere on Nov. 4</a> above the North Sumatra region of Indonesia and largely burned up, an abrupt ending to two decades spent <a href="https://theconversation.com/exploding-stars-send-out-powerful-bursts-of-energy-im-leading-a-citizen-scientist-project-to-classify-and-learn-about-these-bright-flashes-221294">observing powerful cosmic explosions</a>.</p>

<p>Swift’s reentry comes after a failed rescue mission in the summer of 2026. LINK, a commercial robotic spacecraft sent to raise Swift into a safer orbit, <a href="https://spacepolicyonline.com/news/swift-rescue-mission-may-not-have-succeeded-but-no-regrets/">reentered Earth’s atmosphere in September</a>. The machine designed to save a falling satellite burned up first.</p>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=sx6X2OsAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">As a Ph.D. candidate in aerospace engineering</a>, I know that <a href="https://doi.org/10.64628/AAI.xdjcgwa97">rescuing satellites is hard</a>. <a href="https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2026-1921">I research</a> how spacecraft approach and capture satellites, including objects that tumble uncontrollably.</p>

<p>Swift’s loss points to a new hazard for the young industry that repairs, refuels and moves spacecraft around in orbit. If something goes wrong, the spacecraft doing the rescuing can become another problem.</p>

<h2>The rescuer started spinning</h2>

<p>The plan was for LINK to approach Swift, grab it with one of its three robotic arms and fire its thrusters to push the telescope back up to about <a href="https://spacepolicyonline.com/news/swift-reboost-mission-encounters-setback/">373 miles (600 kilometers)</a> above Earth’s surface, where it could keep observing for years.</p>

<p>In late July, <a href="https://www.space.com/space-exploration/missions/nasa-ends-swift-space-telescope-mission-after-failed-rescue-attempt">LINK lost two of its three reaction wheels</a>, which are heavy wheels inside a spacecraft that help it turn without using fuel. That loss, combined with problems with its propulsion system, sent the spacecraft into an uncontrolled spin. </p>

<p>Without working wheels, a spacecraft steers with its thrusters instead, and every burn spends propellant.</p>

<p>Engineers eventually slowed LINK’s rotation by <a href="https://gizmodo.com/nasas-plan-to-save-swift-just-got-a-software-fix-it-badly-needed-2000486000">firing its thrusters against the spin</a>. NASA <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/2026/08/06/link-spacecraft-recovery-progressing-for-nasas-swift-boost/">reported in August</a> that they had cut its spin from about nine degrees per second to roughly one and a half degrees per second.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769913/original/file-20261104-64-7w2ave.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two scientists in protective suits stand in a clean room with lights focused on a box-like spacecraft." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769913/original/file-20261104-64-7w2ave.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769913/original/file-20261104-64-7w2ave.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769913/original/file-20261104-64-7w2ave.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769913/original/file-20261104-64-7w2ave.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769913/original/file-20261104-64-7w2ave.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769913/original/file-20261104-64-7w2ave.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769913/original/file-20261104-64-7w2ave.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Katalyst scientists stand with the LINK spacecraft in April 2026. It launched several months later, in July.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/SatelliteRescueMission/a12dc896151c4b8ea2088205d9271ec2/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=nasa%20link&amp;currentItemNo=0&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">Sophia Roberts/NASA via AP, File</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>NASA and Katalyst Space, LINK’s builder, called off the capture and boost <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/2026/09/04/commercial-spacecraft-for-nasas-swift-boost-continues-tech-demo/">later in August</a>. The team still flew LINK within 7.5 to 9 miles (12 to 15 kilometers) of Swift, where it deployed LINK’s three robotic arms and tested its electric thrusters. It never got close enough to grab the telescope.</p>

<h2>Fuel is the rescue budget</h2>

<p>A servicing spacecraft, like LINK, launches with a finite supply of propellant. Engineers split that fuel supply among the mission’s jobs, from reaching the target and approaching it safely to capturing it and moving it to a new orbit. They also pack some extra fuel in case of surprises.</p>

<p>Think of a tow truck that burns most of its gas getting itself out of a ditch. Even if it reaches a broken-down car, it may not have enough fuel left to tow it home.</p>

<p>That scenario is close to what happened to LINK. Even after engineers brought its spin under control, Katalyst said the spacecraft <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/30/science/nasa-swift-observatory-falling">no longer had enough propellant</a> to capture Swift and raise its orbit safely.</p>

<p>A fuel budget that covers only the planned steps leaves nothing for recovering from a fault. But every extra pound of propellant also makes a spacecraft heavier, and heavier spacecraft cost more to launch and take more fuel to move.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769376/original/file-20261031-64-5v4q00.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A diagram showing two fuel bars, representing how much propellant goes to which tasks and contrasting different fuel budgets." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769376/original/file-20261031-64-5v4q00.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769376/original/file-20261031-64-5v4q00.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=396&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769376/original/file-20261031-64-5v4q00.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=396&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769376/original/file-20261031-64-5v4q00.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=396&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769376/original/file-20261031-64-5v4q00.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=498&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769376/original/file-20261031-64-5v4q00.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=498&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769376/original/file-20261031-64-5v4q00.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=498&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

Illustrative only; not LINK’s actual fuel figures. Original schematic, not to scale.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Wanjiku Chebet Kanjumba, CC BY-NC-ND</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Speed buys time and costs backup</h2>

<p>Starting in 2024, <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/2026/10/23/nasas-swift-mission-ends-ahead-of-re-entry/">solar activity</a> swelled Earth’s upper atmosphere, and the extra drag pulled Swift down faster than expected. Once NASA saw how quickly Swift was falling, the agency had to move fast to try to save the observatory. Space missions typically take years to develop and launch, but in this case, a slow, conventional development program risked arriving too late.</p>

<p>NASA awarded Katalyst a US$30 million contract in September 2025. The company had less than a year <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/mission/swift/swift-boost-mission/timeline/">to design, build, test and launch LINK</a>. LINK launched on July 3, 2026.</p>

<p>Speed comes with trade-offs. In engineering, a compressed schedule can leave less time for repeated testing, building spare hardware and planning recovery options. Public reports do not say whether that trade-off played any part in LINK’s faults.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-updates-next-steps-for-commercial-swift-boost-mission/">NASA has said</a> that even though LINK didn’t succeed, the effort gave the agency experience in quickly building, launching and operating a servicing spacecraft. Engineers also showed they could <a href="https://gizmodo.com/nasas-plan-to-save-swift-just-got-a-software-fix-it-badly-needed-2000486000">upload new control software</a> to steady a damaged servicing spacecraft with the hardware it had left. And LINK <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/2026/09/04/commercial-spacecraft-for-nasas-swift-boost-continues-tech-demo/">tested its arms and fired all three thrusters at once</a> in orbit.</p>



<h2>What comes next</h2>

<p>While Swift was the most pressing case for a boost mission, it’s not the only one. <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble/">NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope</a> could one day use a similar boost, and <a href="https://www.azfamily.com/2026/08/20/nasa-telescope-doomed-after-flagstaff-companys-rescue-attempt-fails/">news reports suggested</a> it would have been next in line had this mission worked.</p>

<p>Future missions are pursuing two complementary approaches for rescuing satellites. Astroscale’s <a href="https://www.space.com/astroscale-elsa-m-space-debris-removal-funding">ELSA-M</a> is built to capture satellites that carry a docking plate installed before launch, which would make it easier for a rescuer to snag and boost them if the satellite eventually got into trouble. The European Space Agency’s <a href="https://www.esa.int/Space_Safety/ClearSpace-1">ClearSpace-1</a> is planned for 2029 and aims to capture the Proba-1 satellite, which doesn’t have a docking plate or anything to help ClearSpace-1 capture it, and remove it from orbit.</p>

<p>LINK’s mission showed that a rescue takes more than a robotic arm and enough thrust to reach a target. It also takes a servicer spacecraft that can stay stable, recover from its own faults and keep enough propellant reserved to finish the job. In Swift’s case, the rescuer fell short before the rescue could begin.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295538/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center/Chris Smith (KBRwyle) NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory took its last look at the sky on Oct. 20, 2026, while orbiting about 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth
NASA ended the telescope’s mission three days later, because Swift had sunk so low that drag from the thin air there meant its telescopes couldn’t hold steady
The telescope reentered the atmosphere on Nov. 4 above the North Sumatra region of Indonesia and largely burned up, an abrupt ending to two decades spent observing powerful cosmic explosions
Swift’s reentry comes after a failed rescue mission in the summer of 2026
LINK, a commercial robotic spacecraft sent to raise Swift into a safer orbit, reentered Earth’s atmosphere in September
The machine designed to save a falling satellite burned up first
As a Ph.D. candidate in aerospace engineering , I know that rescuing satellites is hard
I research how spacecraft approach and capture satellites, including objects that tumble uncontrollably
Swift’s loss points to a new hazard for the young industry that repairs, refuels and moves spacecraft around in orbit
If something goes wrong, the spacecraft doing the rescuing can become another problem

The rescuer started spinning The plan was for LINK to approach Swift, grab it with one of its three robotic arms and fire its thrusters to push the telescope back up to about 373 miles (600 kilometers) above Earth’s surface, where it could keep observing for years
In late July, LINK lost two of its three reaction wheels , which are heavy wheels inside a spacecraft that help it turn without using fuel
That loss, combined with problems with its propulsion system, sent the spacecraft into an uncontrolled spin
Without working wheels, a spacecraft steers with its thrusters instead, and every burn spends propellant
Engineers eventually slowed LINK’s rotation by firing its thrusters against the spin
NASA reported in August that they had cut its spin from about nine degrees per second to roughly one and a half degrees per second
Katalyst scientists stand with the LINK spacecraft in April 2026
It launched several months later, in July
Sophia Roberts/NASA via AP, File NASA and Katalyst Space, LINK’s builder, called off the capture and boost later in August
The team still flew LINK within 7.5 to 9 miles (12 to 15 kilometers) of Swift, where it deployed LINK’s three robotic arms and tested its electric thrusters
It never got close enough to grab the telescope
Fuel is the rescue budget A servicing spacecraft, like LINK, launches with a finite supply of propellant
Engineers split that fuel supply among the mission’s jobs, from reaching the target and approaching it safely to capturing it and moving it to a new orbit
They also pack some extra fuel in case of surprises
Think of a tow truck that burns most of its gas getting itself out of a ditch
Even if it reaches a broken-down car, it may not have enough fuel left to tow it home
That scenario is close to what happened to LINK
Even after engineers brought its spin under control, Katalyst said the spacecraft no longer had enough propellant to capture Swift and raise its orbit safely

<title>Pennsylvania Democrats now have power to push forward on election reform, marijuana legalization and minimum wage increases</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770068/original/file-20261104-64-otg4qd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2435%2C1623&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Democrats, including Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, left, and Lt. Gov. Austin Davis, will have full control of state government in 2027.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Election%202026%20Pennsylvania/4dcb6f52c3944735b2cd3d846f2dfc95/photo">AP Photo/Matt Rourke</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The <a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/2026-midterm-elections-178375">2026 midterm elections</a> <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/04/us/midterm-election-results-democrats">changed the balance of power</a> in Washington, D.C. It also proved to be a pivotal election in Pennsylvania.</p>

<p>Gov. Josh Shapiro <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/pennsylvania-governor-election-results-josh-shapiro-stacy-garrity/">handily defeated</a> Republican challenger Stacy Garrity, the current state treasurer. Not only that, it looks like Democrats <a href="https://apnews.com/projects/elections-2026/pennsylvania-results/">will expand</a> their majority in the state House and have <a href="https://www.inquirer.com/politics/election/inq2/pa-state-house-senate-midterm-election-live-results-20261103.html">flipped the state Senate</a>, earning a 26-24 majority. </p>

<p>That gives Shapiro the coveted party <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/State_government_trifectas">trifecta</a> – single party control of both the governor’s office and the General Assembly. </p>

<p>Given the pent-up demand among Democrats who have not fully controlled Harrisburg <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Party_control_of_Pennsylvania_state_government">for over 30 years</a>, the excitement is palpable among Pennsylvania Democrats. </p>

<p>I teach public policy at Penn State Harrisburg and have a particular interest in <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=NE3FeMgAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">Pennsylvania state politics</a>. Now that the political fault lines are clear for the next two years in Pennsylvania’s state government, it is worth considering what Democrats may do with their newfound power. </p>

<p>For a glimpse at potential Democratic priorities, it is helpful to look at what legislation the current Democrat-controlled House <a href="https://www.pahouse.com/deliveringforpa">has been sending the</a> Republican-controlled Senate.</p>

<h2>Election reform</h2>

<p>Election reform has been a perennial priority in Pennsylvania since the passage of <a href="https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?SESSYR=2019&amp;SESSIND=0&amp;ACTNUM=0077.&amp;CHPT=000.&amp;SCTN=000.&amp;SUBSCTN=000.">Act 77 of 2019</a> and the 2020 election. </p>

<p>Act 77 authorized no-excuse absentee balloting and eliminated straight-ticket voting where voters could vote all at once for a single party, which was <a href="https://www.northcentralpa.com/news/historic-election-reform-bill-including-new-mail-in-voting-signed/article_f11a1a06-fcb9-11e9-b1f5-1b9c92f767de.html">a bipartisan compromise</a> but became a political flash point in President Donald Trump’s efforts to question the 2020 election results. No-excuse means that voters do not need to provide a specific qualifying reason to vote by mail.</p>

<p>Democratic election law priorities have included requiring counties in Pennsylvania to <a href="https://www.votebeat.org/pennsylvania/2025/05/13/voting-election-legislation-voter-identification-mail-ballot-precanvassing/">use ballot drop boxes</a>, maintain <a href="https://www.democracydocket.com/news-alerts/democrats-seek-to-defend-mail-in-voting-from-gop-attack-in-pennsylvania/">no-excuse mail-in voting</a>, set clear rules for <a href="https://www.votebeat.org/pennsylvania/2025/05/13/voting-election-legislation-voter-identification-mail-ballot-precanvassing/">ballot curing</a> where voters are able to correct issues with their submitted mail ballots instead of having them invalidated, institute <a href="https://www.votebeat.org/pennsylvania/2025/05/13/voting-election-legislation-voter-identification-mail-ballot-precanvassing/">precanvassing</a> to speed the counting of absentee ballots, and allow independents to vote in <a href="https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2026/09/pennsylvania-state-house-passes-open-primaries-bill-harrisburg-elections/">open primary elections</a>.</p>

<p>Democrats may now be able to pass all of these without having to compromise with Republican demands for stricter voter ID requirements. </p>

<h2>Marijuana</h2>

<p>Shapiro has repeatedly included revenue projections from adult-use recreational marijuana legalization in his budget proposals, and the House <a href="https://www.mpp.org/states/pennsylvania/">passed a legalization bill in 2025</a>. Democrats had said that <a href="https://whyy.org/articles/pennsylvania-adult-use-marijuana-november-election/">they will legalize recreational marijuana</a> if they took the Senate in 2026. But important details of legalization remain to be worked out, even with Democratic control. </p>

<p>Democrats have sponsored divergent bills on whether sales should be through private dispensaries or <a href="https://theconversation.com/as-pennsylvania-inches-toward-legalizing-recreational-cannabis-lawmakers-propose-selling-it-in-state-owned-dispensaries-similar-to-state-liquor-stores-250368">state stores</a>, similar to how alcohol is sold in Pennsylvania.</p>

<p>Social equity measures meant to repair some of the <a href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/race-mass-incarceration-and-disastrous-war-drugs">harms of the war on drugs</a> on communities disproportionately affected by the criminalization of marijuana will also be key to eventual passage. These include things such as expungements of past convictions, setting aside licenses for minority dispensary owners, and community reinvestment of cannabis tax revenues.</p>

<p>Even with Democratic control, the devil will be in the details. But a Democratic trifecta in Pennsylvania makes it even more likely that the commonwealth will be <a href="https://www.marijuanamoment.net/pennsylvania-is-teed-up-to-finally-legalize-marijuana-as-democrats-claim-majority-in-state-senate/">among the next states</a> where adult-use recreational marijuana is legal.</p>

<h2>Data centers and AI</h2>

<p>The House has passed several measures to regulate artificial intelligence and the data center build-out in the commonwealth. This includes a measure that would <a href="https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb0095">require warnings</a> on advertisements that were made using AI and several that target <a href="https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb1834">energy costs</a>, <a href="https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb2246">water use</a>, <a href="https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb2496">local government authority</a> and <a href="https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb2650">implementing</a> and the <a href="https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2026/08/pennsylvania-data-center-executive-order-shapiro-explainer-environment/">Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development</a> plan. </p>

<p>These measures and others are likely to remain on the Democrats’ agenda. Additionally, criticism over the AI-generated ads <a href="https://www.nbcphiladelphia.com/video/elections/stacy-garrity-josh-shapiro-speak-on-controversial-ai-generated-campaign-ad/4490203/">fielded by the Garrity campaign</a>, which are <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/artificial-intelligence-ai-in-elections-and-campaigns">regulated in other states</a>, may add this issue to the state’s AI policy agenda. </p>

<h2>Affordability</h2>

<p>Given that this election was likely heavily influenced by <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2026/0/as-the-2026-midterms-approach-economy-is-front-and-center/">voters’ concerns about affordability</a>, Democrats will need to show progress on bringing down prices where they can. The Democrats’ <a href="https://pasenate.com/affordability/">Affordability Action Plan</a> includes measures such as property tax and rent rebates, other housing protections for underserved communities, doubling the income tax credit and increasing food and energy security funding.</p>

<p>Another affordability priority for House Democrats since taking control of the chamber in 2023 has been raising the state’s US$7.25 minimum hourly wage over time. The <a href="https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb2189">bill passed by the House</a> in March 2026 would have raised it to $11 in 2027, $13 in 2028 and $15 in 2029, with subsequent annual cost-of-living adjustments, if it also had been passed by the Senate. This is important in Philadelphia, given that <a href="https://www.nbcphiladelphia.com/news/politics/philly-doesnt-have-the-authority-to-raise-its-minimum-wage-heres-why/3530750/">state law prohibits</a> the city from setting its own minimum wage. The legislation will have to be introduced and passed again by the new General Assembly. </p>

<h2>Same-sex marriage and antidiscrimination</h2>

<p>Same-sex marriage equality may seem like a settled issue with the 2015 <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/2014/14-556">Obergefell v. Hodges decision</a> by the U.S. Supreme Court, but the 2022 <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/2021/19-1392">overturning</a> of <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/1971/70-18">Roe v. Wade</a> by today’s more conservative court has sparked concerns of further changes to precedent. </p>

<p>Pennsylvania’s statutory definition of marriage is still between “one man and one woman,” something that a bipartisan majority in the House <a href="https://www.palegis.us/legislation/bills/2025/hb1800">tried to change in 2026</a> to “two individuals.”  Democrats are very likely to pick this back up and may even attempt a more durable, but also <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Constitution">more procedurally difficult</a>, constitutional amendment that enshrines same-sex marriage rights. </p>

<p>Pennsylvania also does not include LGBTQ individuals in its nondiscrimination protections. The Democrats in the House <a href="https://www.cityandstatepa.com/policy/2026/04/house-passes-bill-would-enshrine-lgbtq-nondiscrimination-protections-state-law/413184/">passed a bill</a> that would add sexual orientation and gender identity to the state’s Human Relations Act in 2026, but it also died in the Senate. Democrats are likely to pick this up again in 2027. </p>

<p>Ultimately, Democrats will not be able to do everything. They will need to decide what to prioritize and what to leave behind. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">

body: Austin Davis, will have full control of state government in 2027
AP Photo/Matt Rourke The 2026 midterm elections changed the balance of power in Washington, D.C
It also proved to be a pivotal election in Pennsylvania
Josh Shapiro handily defeated Republican challenger Stacy Garrity, the current state treasurer
Not only that, it looks like Democrats will expand their majority in the state House and have flipped the state Senate , earning a 26-24 majority
That gives Shapiro the coveted party trifecta – single party control of both the governor’s office and the General Assembly
Given the pent-up demand among Democrats who have not fully controlled Harrisburg for over 30 years , the excitement is palpable among Pennsylvania Democrats
I teach public policy at Penn State Harrisburg and have a particular interest in Pennsylvania state politics
Now that the political fault lines are clear for the next two years in Pennsylvania’s state government, it is worth considering what Democrats may do with their newfound power
For a glimpse at potential Democratic priorities, it is helpful to look at what legislation the current Democrat-controlled House has been sending the Republican-controlled Senate
Eileen Hartnett Albillar, a social worker and clerk of courts, beat Republican incumbent state Sen
Frank Farry in the 6th Senatorial District in Bucks County, Pa
AP Photo/Matt Rourke Election reform Election reform has been a perennial priority in Pennsylvania since the passage of Act 77 of 2019 and the 2020 election

Act 77 authorized no-excuse absentee balloting and eliminated straight-ticket voting where voters could vote all at once for a single party, which was a bipartisan compromise but became a political flash point in President Donald Trump’s efforts to question the 2020 election results
No-excuse means that voters do not need to provide a specific qualifying reason to vote by mail

Democratic election law priorities have included requiring counties in Pennsylvania to use ballot drop boxes , maintain no-excuse mail-in voting , set clear rules for ballot curing where voters are able to correct issues with their submitted mail ballots instead of having them invalidated, institute precanvassing to speed the counting of absentee ballots, and allow independents to vote in open primary elections
Democrats may now be able to pass all of these without having to compromise with Republican demands for stricter voter ID requirements
Marijuana Shapiro has repeatedly included revenue projections from adult-use recreational marijuana legalization in his budget proposals, and the House passed a legalization bill in 2025
Democrats had said that they will legalize recreational marijuana if they took the Senate in 2026
But important details of legalization remain to be worked out, even with Democratic control
Democrats have sponsored divergent bills on whether sales should be through private dispensaries or state stores , similar to how alcohol is sold in Pennsylvania
Social equity measures meant to repair some of the harms of the war on drugs on communities disproportionately affected by the criminalization of marijuana will also be key to eventual passage
These include things such as expungements of past convictions, setting aside licenses for minority dispensary owners, and community reinvestment of cannabis tax revenues
Even with Democratic control, the devil will be in the details
But a Democratic trifecta in Pennsylvania makes it even more likely that the commonwealth will be among the next states where adult-use recreational marijuana is legal
Voters wait in line to vote at Central Bucks South High School on Election Day in Warrington, Pa., on Nov. 3, 2026
AP Photo/Matt Rourke Data centers and AI The House has passed several measures to regulate artificial intelligence and the data center build-out in the commonwealth

This includes a measure that would require warnings on advertisements that were made using AI and several that target energy costs , water use , local government authority and implementing and the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development plan
These measures and others are likely to remain on the Democrats’ agenda
Additionally, criticism over the AI-generated ads fielded by the Garrity campaign , which are regulated in other states , may add this issue to the state’s AI policy agenda
Affordability Given that this election was likely heavily influenced by voters’ concerns about affordability , Democrats will need to show progress on bringing down prices where they can

The Democrats’ Affordability Action Plan includes measures such as property tax and rent rebates, other housing protections for underserved communities, doubling the income tax credit and increasing food and energy security funding
Another affordability priority for House Democrats since taking control of the chamber in 2023 has been raising the state’s US$7.25 minimum hourly wage over time

The bill passed by the House in March 2026 would have raised it to $11 in 2027, $13 in 2028 and $15 in 2029, with subsequent annual cost-of-living adjustments, if it also had been passed by the Senate
This is important in Philadelphia, given that state law prohibits the city from setting its own minimum wage
The legislation will have to be introduced and passed again by the new General Assembly
Same-sex marriage and antidiscrimination Same-sex marriage equality may seem like a settled issue with the 2015 Obergefell v
Supreme Court, but the 2022 overturning of Roe v
Wade by today’s more conservative court has sparked concerns of further changes to precedent

Pennsylvania’s statutory definition of marriage is still between “one man and one woman,” something that a bipartisan majority in the House tried to change in 2026 to “two individuals.” Democrats are very likely to pick this back up and may even attempt a more durable, but also more procedurally difficult , constitutional amendment that enshrines same-sex marriage rights

title: Midterms are bad for incumbents – and even worse when energy prices are high
url:
<title>Midterms are bad for incumbents – and even worse when energy prices are high</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770048/original/file-20261104-78-v9782u.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7453%2C4968&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Voters respond to economic and political messages and experiences.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Election2026AmericaVotesAlaska/269c61c8a3ee4d729b895d56f17a0618/photo">AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>As Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “<a href="https://politicaldictionary.com/words/its-the-economy-stupid/">It’s the economy, stupid</a>.” Democratic strategist James Carville famously said that to presidential candidate Bill Clinton in 1992, but he might have said “it’s energy prices” instead. <a href="https://theconversation.com/iran-war-pushes-diesel-the-economys-lifeblood-to-record-high-prices-with-no-relief-on-the-horizon-292049">The cost of energy underlies much of the economy</a>, making energy and politics inseparable, especially when gasoline prices rise. </p>

<p>Midterm elections have historically been <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1532673X251325458">difficult for incumbent presidents</a> and <a href="https://www.scrippsnews.com/politics/midterm-elections/why-does-the-president-s-party-typically-lose-midterms">often shift</a> the <a href="https://riponsociety.org/article/the-midterm-curse-and-the-balance-of-power-in-washington/">balance of power</a> in Washington, D.C. </p>

<p>Many factors affecting gasoline prices are beyond a president’s or Congress’s control. Prices for crude oil and petroleum <a href="https://pumptex.com/6-interesting-facts-about-gas-stations.php">products such as gasoline</a> are <a href="https://www.investopedia.com/articles/economics/08/determining-oil-prices.asp">set on global markets</a> as the results of economic forces of supply and demand. Even the companies that produce oil don’t have <a href="https://www.afpm.org/newsroom/blog/do-refineries-set-price-gasoline">as much influence as people might think</a>, because of how that oil gets to refineries: Over 60% of the world’s crude oil is <a href="https://understand-energy.stanford.edu/news/understand-oil-trade-and-transportation">transported by ocean tankers</a>, with 20% of global supplies <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=65504">traveling through the Strait of Hormuz</a>, which has been closed, or nearly so, for much of 2026 as the conflict with Iran drags on.</p>

<p>When <a href="https://theconversation.com/iran-war-pushes-diesel-the-economys-lifeblood-to-record-high-prices-with-no-relief-on-the-horizon-292049">energy prices rise, other prices, such as food</a>, follow. <a href="https://www.dallasfed.org/-/media/documents/research/papers/2022/wp2224.pdf">Sudden spikes in gasoline prices</a> can contribute to <a href="https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/inflationary-impact-energy-prices">higher inflation, both regionally</a> <a href="https://nypost.com/2026/10/29/business/feds-preferred-inflation-gauge-heats-up-over-high-gas-prices/">and nationally</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1532673X251325458">Voters pay attention</a> to those changes, and <a href="https://www.spglobal.com/energy/en/news-research/latest-news/crude-oil/062624-us-elections-gasoline-price-fluctuations-could-play-role-in-2024-presidential-election">incumbents are less likely to win reelection</a>. For the 2026 midterm election, <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/02/gas-prices-are-set-be-highest-any-election-day-us-history/">gasoline prices were the highest</a> of any previous election. That put Republicans in the precarious position of <a href="https://thehill.com/policy/energy-environment/6173484-republicans-high-gas-prices-voters-midterms">defending their record</a>. </p>

<p>Four American presidents – Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan and Joe Biden – confronted the <a href="https://grist.org/politics/jimmy-carter-legacy-energy-american-politics/">consequences of severe inflation and high fuel prices</a> during midterm elections. </p>

<p><iframe id="bDmPk" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/bDmPk/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A bar chart showing crude oil prices, gas prices and election results in midterm election years."></iframe></p>

<h2>Oil embargo, Nixon and Ford</h2>

<p>Richard Nixon was the first modern president to truly face an energy crisis that became political. In retaliation for U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Yom Kippur War, Arab members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries <a href="https://history.state.gov/milestones/1969-1976/oil-embargo">cut oil production and imposed an oil embargo</a> on the United States. <a href="https://www.bakerinstitute.org/research/arab-embargo-50-years-ago-weaponized-oil-inflict-economic-trauma-sound-familiar">OPEC oil production fell by 5% a month</a>, and crude oil prices rocketed 184% from prewar levels of <a href="https://www.macrotrends.net/1369/crude-oil-price-history-chart">$4.31 to $10.31 per barrel</a> in March 1974. Nixon’s <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/93rd-congress/house-bill/8863">federal price controls on petroleum</a> didn’t prevent U.S. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/browser/index.php?tbl=T09.04#/?f=M&amp;start=197301&amp;end=202609&amp;charted=5-10-11">gasoline prices from increasing 32%</a>.</p>

<p>When Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, Gerald Ford took office. <a href="https://www.investopedia.com/inflation-rate-by-year-7253832">Inflation was 12.3%</a>, and <a href="https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/browser/index.php?tbl=T09.04#/?f=M&amp;start=197301&amp;end=202609&amp;charted=5-10-11">gas prices were still high</a>.  </p>

<p>Right before that year’s midterm election, Ford launched the “<a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/win-how-gerald-ford-tried-to-whip-inflation-with-a-button/">Whip Inflation Now</a>,” or WIN, campaign. But <a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/statistics/data/seats-congress-gainedlost-the-presidents-party-mid-term-elections">Republicans lost 48 House seats</a> and five Senate seats. </p>

<p>“WIN” didn’t work, and by the 1976 presidential election, gas prices were <a href="https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/browser/index.php?tbl=T09.04#/?f=M&amp;start=197507&amp;end=197611&amp;charted=5-10-11">over 60 cents a gallon</a> – adjusted for inflation to late 2026, that’s $3.49. Ford lost his reelection bid to Jimmy Carter.</p>

<p><iframe id="lsq39" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/lsq39/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A column chart showing the annual inflation rates in the U.S. from 1929 to 2026."></iframe></p>

<h2>Carter’s struggles</h2>

<p>In Carter’s first two years in office, starting in 1977, the monthly average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/browser/index.php?tbl=T09.04#/?f=M&amp;start=197612&amp;end=198101&amp;charted=5-10-11">stayed high and even climbed slightly</a>. Inflation hit <a href="https://www.investopedia.com/inflation-rate-by-year-7253832">9% in 1978</a>. </p>

<p>In the 1978 midterm election, <a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/statistics/data/seats-congress-gainedlost-the-presidents-party-mid-term-elections">Democrats lost 15 House and three Senate seats</a>. <a href="https://www.investopedia.com/inflation-rate-by-year-7253832">Inflation continued to climb</a>, and by the 1980 presidential election, gas prices were <a href="https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/browser/index.php?tbl=T09.04#/?f=M&amp;start=197507&amp;end=197611&amp;charted=5-10-11">twice what they had been in 1976</a>. Plagued by those figures and the Iranian hostage crisis, Carter lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan. </p>

<p><iframe id="bmTZY" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/bmTZY/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A line chart showing the gas prices in nominal and inflation-adjusted figures from 1992 to 2026."></iframe></p>

<h2>Reagan enters the picture</h2>

<p>Reagan implemented “<a href="https://www.law.georgetown.edu/denny-center/blog/reaganomics/">Reaganomics</a>” by cutting taxes and regulations, reducing government spending, tightening monetary policy and <a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/executive-order-12287-decontrol-crude-oil-and-refined-petroleum-products">removing the remaining price controls on petroleum</a>. By the mid-1980s, <a href="https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/leafhandler.ashx?n=pet&amp;s=mcrfpus2&amp;f=m">increased oil production from U.S.</a> and non-OPEC nations <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1981/06/21/business/how-the-oil-glut-is-changing-business.html">led to an oil glut</a>, lowering the <a href="https://www.macrotrends.net/1369/crude-oil-price-history-chart">average price of crude oil</a> and <a href="https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/browser/index.php?tbl=T09.04#/?f=M&amp;start=198009&amp;end=198902&amp;charted=5-10-11">U.S. gasoline price from previous highs</a>. </p>

<p>In the 1982 midterms, <a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/statistics/data/seats-congress-gainedlost-the-presidents-party-mid-term-elections">Republicans lost 26 seats in the House</a> and gained one in the Senate. </p>

<p>Reagan won reelection to the presidency in a landslide in 1984, but the challenges for incumbents remained in the 1986 midterms. Though <a href="https://www.macrotrends.net/1369/crude-oil-price-history-chart">crude oil prices were $15 a barrel</a> and <a href="https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/browser/index.php?tbl=T09.04#/?f=M&amp;start=198009&amp;end=198902&amp;charted=5-10-11">gas had dropped to 82 cents</a> a gallon, <a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/statistics/data/seats-congress-gainedlost-the-presidents-party-mid-term-elections">Republicans lost five seats in the House</a> and eight in the Senate. </p>

<h2>Trump’s first round</h2>

<p>In the lead-up to the midterms during Donald Trump’s first term as president, crude prices had <a href="https://www.macrotrends.net/1369/crude-oil-price-history-chart">risen about 24%</a> from when he took office in January 2017 to October 2018. And <a href="https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/monthly/index.php">gas prices were up 22%</a>. In the 2018 midterms, Republicans <a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/statistics/data/seats-congress-gainedlost-the-presidents-party-mid-term-elections">lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769851/original/file-20261103-65-lsyatu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="People gathered in a room hug and smile." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769851/original/file-20261103-65-lsyatu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769851/original/file-20261103-65-lsyatu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769851/original/file-20261103-65-lsyatu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769851/original/file-20261103-65-lsyatu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769851/original/file-20261103-65-lsyatu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769851/original/file-20261103-65-lsyatu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769851/original/file-20261103-65-lsyatu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Democratic Party supporters react to the results of the 2018 midterm elections, when their party won control of the U.S. House of Representatives.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/people-cheer-while-watching-election-results-during-a-news-photo/1058470780">Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Biden years</h2>

<p>Over the course of 2020, COVID-19 restrictions slowed the U.S. economy. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/leafhandler.ashx?n=pet&amp;s=mcrfpus2&amp;f=m">U.S. crude oil production fell</a> as <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=46141">gasoline demand plummeted by 40%</a>. Prices rose because of pandemic-related supply chain backups.</p>

<p>And from Election Day in November 2020 to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. rose by 66%, <a href="https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/browser/index.php?tbl=T09.04#/?f=M&amp;start=200001">from $2.11 to $3.52 per gallon</a>. </p>

<p>Also, as pandemic restrictions lifted and the economy began recovering, demand for gasoline rebounded, straining supplies. </p>

<p>Upon taking office in 2021, Biden took steps to curb rising energy costs, including <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/business-60936468">releasing  oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve</a> in March 2022, which the Treasury Department suggested helped prevent gasoline price increases of <a href="https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jy0887">$0.17 to $0.42 per gallon</a>.</p>

<p>But other Biden policy moves made it harder to increase energy supplies. He <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2021/06/09/tc-energy-terminates-keystone-xl-pipeline-project.html">canceled the Keystone XL pipeline project</a> that would have brought more petroleum into the U.S. and <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/LSB11259">suspended new oil and gas leases</a> in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the Gulf of Mexico. He also <a href="https://2021-2025.state.gov/the-united-states-officially-rejoins-the-paris-agreement/">recommitted the U.S. to the Paris climate accord</a>, under which countries have promised to cut their greenhouse gas emissions, generally meaning moving away from fossil fuels as an energy source. </p>

<p>In June 2022, <a href="https://www.investopedia.com/us-inflation-rate-by-president-8546447">inflation reached 9.1%</a>, a 40-year high. And U.S. gasoline prices reached an <a href="https://www.eia.gov/totalenergy/data/browser/index.php?tbl=T09.04#/?f=M&amp;start=200001">all-time high of $4.929 per gallon</a>; adjusted for inflation, that’s $5.60 a gallon today. </p>

<p>The 2022 midterm election wasn’t as bad for Democrats as they might have feared, though it wasn’t a success: The party <a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/statistics/data/seats-congress-gainedlost-the-presidents-party-mid-term-elections">lost nine House seats</a> and one Senate seat. That’s a reminder that <a href="https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2022/10/drives-american-voters">energy prices aren’t the only factor</a> in voters’ minds when they are casting ballots.</p>

<h2>Trump’s second term</h2>

<p>During the first 12 months of Trump’s second term, <a href="https://www.macrotrends.net/1369/crude-oil-price-history-chart">crude oil prices fell 4.5%</a>,  U.S. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/leafhandler.ashx?n=pet&amp;s=mcrfpus2&amp;f=m">oil production rose 3.3%</a>, from 13.3 million to 13.7 million barrels per day, and the AAA national average price of regular unleaded gasoline fell 4.5%, <a href="https://gasprices.aaa.com/2025/02/">from $3.12</a> to <a href="https://gasprices.aaa.com/2026/02/">$2.98 per gallon</a>.</p>

<p>On Feb. 28, 2026, U.S. military action against Iran disrupted Middle Eastern oil production and oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Initially, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/01/crude-oil-exports-strait-of-hormuz-transport-gulf-region-diesel">shipment volume plummeted</a>, though by the end of September it had <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/30/iran-war-strait-hormuz-gulf-oil-fuel.html">recovered to 82% to 92% of prewar levels</a>.</p>

<p>Overall, Middle Eastern crude oil exports are averaging around 24 million barrels a day, <a href="https://www.wsj.com/world/middle-east/more-oil-is-now-coming-out-of-the-persian-gulf-than-before-the-iran-war-6a6d1670">exceeding prewar levels</a> in part because of increased use of pipelines out of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Because of the war with Iran, AAA’s national average price of unleaded regular gasoline has increased by almost 40%, from <a href="https://gasprices.aaa.com/2026/01/">February’s $2.98 price</a> to <a href="https://gasprices.aaa.com">$4.15 a gallon</a> as of Nov. 3, 2026.</p>

<h2>Implications</h2>

<p>As the preelection polling had suggested, voters held Trump accountable for <a href="https://poll.qu.edu/poll-release?releaseid=3956">high gasoline and grocery prices</a>, as well as <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/10/08/iran-conflict-remains-deeply-unpopular-as-many-americans-expect-it-to-go-on-for-months/">an unpopular war</a>.</p>

<p>It was a reminder of a basic economic and political principle: When the economy is doing well, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.electstud.2010.09.001">voters are more likely to support incumbents</a> and their parties. And when voters are <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/guide/midterm-elections-economy-affordability/">pessimistic about the economy’s future</a>, they are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-3816.00063">inclined to vote against incumbents</a> and their parties.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295287/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

excerpt: Voters respond to economic and political messages and experiences
body: Voters respond to economic and political messages and experiences

AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson As Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “ It’s the economy, stupid .” Democratic strategist James Carville famously said that to presidential candidate Bill Clinton in 1992, but he might have said “it’s energy prices” instead
The cost of energy underlies much of the economy , making energy and politics inseparable, especially when gasoline prices rise
Midterm elections have historically been difficult for incumbent presidents and often shift the balance of power in Washington, D.C
Many factors affecting gasoline prices are beyond a president’s or Congress’s control
Prices for crude oil and petroleum products such as gasoline are set on global markets as the results of economic forces of supply and demand

Even the companies that produce oil don’t have as much influence as people might think , because of how that oil gets to refineries: Over 60% of the world’s crude oil is transported by ocean tankers , with 20% of global supplies traveling through the Strait of Hormuz , which has been closed, or nearly so, for much of 2026 as the conflict with Iran drags on
When energy prices rise, other prices, such as food , follow
Sudden spikes in gasoline prices can contribute to higher inflation, both regionally and nationally
Voters pay attention to those changes, and incumbents are less likely to win reelection
For the 2026 midterm election, gasoline prices were the highest of any previous election
That put Republicans in the precarious position of defending their record
Four American presidents – Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan and Joe Biden – confronted the consequences of severe inflation and high fuel prices during midterm elections
Oil embargo, Nixon and Ford Richard Nixon was the first modern president to truly face an energy crisis that became political

In retaliation for U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Yom Kippur War, Arab members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries cut oil production and imposed an oil embargo on the United States
OPEC oil production fell by 5% a month , and crude oil prices rocketed 184% from prewar levels of $4.31 to $10.31 per barrel in March 1974
Nixon’s federal price controls on petroleum didn’t prevent U.S. gasoline prices from increasing 32%
When Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, Gerald Ford took office
Inflation was 12.3% , and gas prices were still high
Right before that year’s midterm election, Ford launched the “ Whip Inflation Now ,” or WIN, campaign

But Republicans lost 48 House seats and five Senate seats. “WIN” didn’t work, and by the 1976 presidential election, gas prices were over 60 cents a gallon – adjusted for inflation to late 2026, that’s $3.49
Ford lost his reelection bid to Jimmy Carter
Carter’s struggles In Carter’s first two years in office, starting in 1977, the monthly average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. stayed high and even climbed slightly
In the 1978 midterm election, Democrats lost 15 House and three Senate seats
Inflation continued to climb , and by the 1980 presidential election, gas prices were twice what they had been in 1976
Plagued by those figures and the Iranian hostage crisis, Carter lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan

Reagan enters the picture Reagan implemented “ Reaganomics ” by cutting taxes and regulations, reducing government spending, tightening monetary policy and removing the remaining price controls on petroleum
By the mid-1980s, increased oil production from U.S. and non-OPEC nations led to an oil glut , lowering the average price of crude oil and U.S. gasoline price from previous highs
In the 1982 midterms, Republicans lost 26 seats in the House and gained one in the Senate
Reagan won reelection to the presidency in a landslide in 1984, but the challenges for incumbents remained in the 1986 midterms
Though crude oil prices were $15 a barrel and gas had dropped to 82 cents a gallon, Republicans lost five seats in the House and eight in the Senate
Trump’s first round In the lead-up to the midterms during Donald Trump’s first term as president, crude prices had risen about 24% from when he took office in January 2017 to October 2018
In the 2018 midterms, Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate
Democratic Party supporters react to the results of the 2018 midterm elections, when their party won control of the U.S
Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images Biden years Over the course of 2020, COVID-19 restrictions slowed the U.S. economy
U.S. crude oil production fell as gasoline demand plummeted by 40%
Prices rose because of pandemic-related supply chain backups
And from Election Day in November 2020 to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. rose by 66%, from $2.11 to $3.52 per gallon
Also, as pandemic restrictions lifted and the economy began recovering, demand for gasoline rebounded, straining supplies

Upon taking office in 2021, Biden took steps to curb rising energy costs, including releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in March 2022, which the Treasury Department suggested helped prevent gasoline price increases of $0.17 to $0.42 per gallon
