title: Donald Trump would like to change the subject
excerpt: President Donald Trump speaks at the site of the White House ballroom on November 4, 2026. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff
body: President Donald Trump speaks at the site of the White House ballroom on November 4, 2026. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s midterms response is a shrug
What happened? By now, you certainly know: Democrats won overwhelmingly in Tuesday’s midterm elections, and they won everywhere

The party will head into 2027 with commanding majorities in the House and the Senate, breaking two years of unified Republican control in Washington, DC.  The results are a sweeping repudiation of Trump, the Republican Party, and the first two years of his second administration
But you wouldn’t know it from the president’s only public appearance on Wednesday, which focused on his beloved East Wing ballroom
How is Trump responding? To a surprising extent, he’s not

He blamed the loss on Republican candidates and his absence from the ballot in social media posts Tuesday night, but his public comments have been subdued, with none of the claims of election fraud that have become his hallmark.  One Trump adviser, according to CNN , said that Trump likely would not attempt to challenge the results (Alaska notwithstanding, potentially) because the scale of the Democratic victories was “too big to rig.” On Wednesday, Trump gave remarks from inside the partially completed ballroom — dwelling on its size, the kitchen setup, and his choice of marble for the flooring — and signed his name on a steel beam

His only comments on the midterms came in response to questions from the press, including about the Iran war, which Vice President JD Vance has blamed for the GOP loss. “I think it’s largely true,” Trump said, “but at the same time, if I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again.” What’s the big picture? It’s pretty likely that we’ll see a few different versions of Trump’s response in the coming days, not to mention when Democrats actually take power in January — my colleague Astead Herndon described it on Wednesday as Trump’s “stages of grief.”  Whatever the next two years look like, though, his tepid response to a historic defeat makes one thing clear: Donald Trump’s time at the center of American politics is slipping away

And with that, it’s time to log off… Another result of Tuesday’s elections: More than a million low-income Texans could soon have access to healthcare , after Democratic victories in the state opened up the possibility of Medicaid expansion
You can read all about it from my colleague Dylan Scott here with a gift link
Or, if you’re ready to be done with politics content for today, here’s a picture of a baby muskox.  Have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!

title: How Democrats won the Deep South
excerpt: Jackson State University students cheer and hold posters of civil rights leader Fannie Lou Hamer as they march across campus on Election Day in Jackson, Mississ
body: Jackson State University students cheer and hold posters of civil rights leader Fannie Lou Hamer as they march across campus on Election Day in Jackson, Mississippi. | Azariah Wells/Jackson State University via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
Many a pundit spent this morning with his or her thesaurus, seeking aquatic metaphors more portentous than “wave.” Call it a blue deluge
Whatever you call last night’s historic rout , the political class is still working through the flotsam and jetsam today
Democrats won not only the US House and Senate, but governorships, state legislatures, and a slew of other down-ballot offices across the country
Democrats were favored to take the House, of course — but not to win this dramatically across the board
Over the past several months, voters have expressed mounting frustration with Republicans and the Trump administration on issues including corruption , the war in Iran, and the runaway cost of living
Last night’s results suggest those issues did get people to the polls: Nearly nine in 10 voters said the cost of living was a major factor in their vote, for instance

But there was also a surprise sleeper issue here — a triumph of mobilization over manipulation, if you will.   In red states across the country, Republicans sought to redraw congressional districts to give themselves a leg up
And that project appears to have backfired, thanks in large part to Black voters
Go a little deeper View Link Consider the extraordinary case of Mississippi, a deep-red state that the national Democratic Party all but abandoned this cycle
The Magnolia State has not elected a Democratic senator since 1982 , and the party’s chances since then have not exactly gotten brighter

Republicans control the Mississippi legislature, governor’s mansion, and both US Senate seats, plus three of its four congressional districts.  But as of 5 pm ET on Wednesday, Scott Colom — the Democrat running for Senate — leads the incumbent Republican by fewer than 100 (!) votes

Win or lose, that showing far exceeds what most pundits even thought possible. “This is all a reaction to voting rights,” explains Vox’s editorial director Benjy Sarlin. “Yes, people are mad about prices
But voting rights was also a huge motivator.” Ironically, the GOP seems to have created this particular problem for itself

After the Supreme Court rolled back voting-rights protections this spring, including restrictions on gerrymandering, Republican leaders in Mississippi began the controversial process of drawing new electoral maps
That process threatened to dilute the state’s Black vote across multiple districts and eliminate the seat of its only Black representative.  Black voters revolted. “People are fired up
They’re incredibly engaged,” one Mississippi reporter told Vox’s Astead Herndon

Colom, the Democratic Senate candidate, even made voting rights a powerful centerpiece of his campaign’s closing argument.  Early reports suggest that message resonated: One voting rights group said that Black turnout in Mississippi might even rival the group’s turnout in the 2008 presidential election

In parts of the state on Tuesday, Black voters “overwhelmed” the polls .  We can’t say for sure that these voters were reacting to redistricting, of course — but turnout was consistently high in majority-Black counties across Mississippi and the broader Deep South
It was “ especially pronounced ,” per the NAACP, in states that redrew their maps this year
Colom was, after all, not the only Democrat to far exceed expectations in a Southern state

In Georgia, Texas, Alabama, and North and South Carolina, Democrats won races they weren’t expected to win or won by vastly larger margins than polls had suggested.  Georgia’s governor-elect, Keisha Lance Bottoms, scored 54.3 percent of the vote in what was supposed to be a neck-and-neck contest
Jon Ossoff bested his challenger by a walloping  18-point margin
In North Carolina, Dems not only picked up a Senate seat with almost 60 percent of the vote, but they  also won House races in districts that had been redrawn to favor Republicans
Even Louisiana — Louisiana! — almost elected a Democrat to the Senate
In the process, these states have opened up what my colleagues dub “ a new era of American politics ”: one that scrambles old assumptions about which voters, and which states, belong to each party
It’s a pretty heady time for Democrats.  The question now is whether they can hold that coalition even after the proverbial floodwaters recede
One link for later ➨ You actually can buy happiness

At least for other people! A 2025 report from the Happier Lives Institute, a research organization founded by the Oxford University philosopher Michael Plant, ranks world charities by how much their work increases life satisfaction in the populations they serve

It’s a helpful frame for thinking about your own charitable donations.  Before you go… Did you know… that paper currency has existed since the 10th century ? China first got that paper, as the kids say, during the Song Dynasty.  Today’s trivia: Which massive e-commerce website explicitly bars its users from selling their souls? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the dog breed beloved by both Rob Zombie and Queen Victoria
That would be the pug, which, as of last year, ranked as the 38th most popular dog in America.

title: Whose fault is the GOP’s cataclysmic defeat? 3 theories are gaining steam on the right.
excerpt: Vice President JD Vance speaks to the media outside Air Force Two on November 2, 2026 in Joint Base Andrews, Maryland. | Tom Brenner/Getty Images Republicans be
body: Vice President JD Vance speaks to the media outside Air Force Two on November 2, 2026 in Joint Base Andrews, Maryland. | Tom Brenner/Getty Images Republicans began picking through their party’s post-midterms wreckage Wednesday to ask about — and argue over — how things went so, so wrong in President Donald Trump’s second term

Tuesday’s blue tsunami not only washed out Republicans’ House and Senate majorities, it carried Democrats into office even in deep red strongholds like South Carolina, Kansas, and possibly Mississippi
It seemed to be a decisive thumbs down from the electorate on the second Trump administration

These results also mark the effective start of the battle to determine what the Republican Party will become after Trump — both who the 2028 GOP presidential nominee will be, and what the party will stand for overall

Within hours of the results, a sort of narrative warfare began to unfold, as different politicians, advocates, and factions tried to advance their preferred accounts of what exactly went wrong, who should get the blame, and what the party should change for the future
Here are three theories of what went wrong that are already starting arguments between big names on the right

Was the war by far the most important thing – or just one problem among many? The conversation about what went wrong is especially important for Vice President JD Vance, who remains the frontrunner for the GOP presidential nomination, but is inextricably tied to an administration that increasingly looks like a failure
So it was noteworthy that he offered his own account of what happened

Vance’s post-mortem glancingly mentioned a few issues, such as “cost of living/inflation,” and floated that he’d be open to changing immigration “enforcement” (though he reiterated he’d never support “amnesty”)

He also cited voters’ belief that the United States should “change our relationship to Israel,” perhaps helping explain why Trump announced on Election Day that he’d decided to end aid to Israel after this year
Yet there was one factor Vance wanted to be sure got most of the blame: the Iran war. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote

What’s more, he claimed that “everyone knows” that is the case, and that “any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” That position is no surprise coming from Vance, who has long been a critic of the hawkish GOP foreign policy establishment, and who had hoped to help steer Trump’s second term on a different course.  Vance is associated with an “America First” faction that was deeply skeptical of US involvement in foreign conflicts, particularly in Ukraine and Iran
But Trump ignored their advice, sided with the hawks, and launched his Iran war early this year

And though Vance stood by that decision publicly, he now wants it known that he was right all along.  Curt Mills, executive director of the American Conservative magazine and a critic of the hawks, told me Wednesday that Vance had a tremendous opportunity to help negotiate an end to the conflict: “He’s in a pole position to get us out of this mistake, and I think if he does do that, he will be associated with ending the war, not starting the war.” The right’s internal conflict between the hawks and the America Firsters, has long been bitter and personal, and goes beyond Vance

Aspects of it played out publicly among commentators Wednesday, with hawks like talk radio host Mark Levin deriding the idea that the war sank Trump.  “The mid-terms were not lost over a single issue.  And anybody with a functioning brain knows that,” Levin posted on X
He added that, to the extent the war harmed Trump politically, it was the fault of the America Firsters’ campaign to “undermine” it

But right-wing commentator Ryan James Girdusky argued to me that the war hurt Trump’s coalition beyond just driving up energy prices. “In 2024, TikTok was all, ‘Trump is great, Trump is the man,’” he said. “What’s the vibe on TikTok today? It’s, ‘You’re at war for Israel.’ That is a completely different narrative, and that’s a mainstream narrative on TikTok.” Is this outcome a rejection of Trumpism – that necessitates something very different? Another narrative some began advancing was that the midterm elections were a repudiation of Trumpism in general — and, particularly, all the ways Trump deviated from the GOP’s pre-Trump conservative principles.  The exact specifics varied, but the conservative commentator Erick Erickson summed up the gist of it by writing : It was gas prices
The accidental arrests of American citizens who were Hispanic

John Curtis (R-UT), who criticized “a hastily executed war, headline after headline of scandals, a ballooning $40 trillion debt, and unpredictable tariffs” while saying it was “time for Republicans to return to the principled conservative values that once defined us—and that we’ve steadily abandoned over the last decade.” Florida Gov
Ron DeSantis, a past and perhaps future Republican presidential candidate, had some pointed criticisms for the Trump administration even before the results were in

This week, he said that in addition to failures on affordability and the Iran war being a “big, big drag,” the administration’s aggressive approach to immigration under former Homeland Secretary Kristi Noem had created “unnecessary” conflicts.  But DeSantis also emphasized another issue: corruption.“ This swamp here is the worst it’s ever been ,” he said. “Look at the amount of money these people are making, who are in the administration,” he went on, specifically calling out Trump lawyer Alina Habba for reportedly getting a $10 million a year contract while advising the Justice Department

Then on Wednesday, DeSantis gave a lengthy press conference in which he portrayed the results as “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans.” Again, he cited the cost of living and corruption, and said that he himself does not trade any stocks while he’s in elected office
What can Republicans do about the economy? There was widespread agreement on the right that Trump had failed to address voters’ concerns about affordability and high prices
There was much less agreement on why, exactly, Trump had failed on the economy — and what Republicans should do instead
To the GOP’s free market faction, Trump had blundered with his tariffs, which, in addition to being handled chaotically, helped drive prices up
Curtis, the senator from Utah, mentioned tariffs and a failure to address the debt as major errors from the administration
Those sympathetic to the populist right were more reluctant to blame the tariffs per se

Gidurksy told me that “the tariffs didn’t do what the anti-tariff audience said they were going to do” — that they did not cause economic catastrophe or raise prices as much as economists had predicted.  Indeed, beyond the tariffs, many on the populist right believe that the Trump administration’s true failure was not delivering on their economic populist rhetoric

For instance, Trump’s biggest legislative accomplishment — the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — was mostly orthodox conservative Republican policy, focused on cutting taxes (particularly for the wealthy) and paying for it by slashing Medicaid and SNAP benefits
But outside a couple of working-class flourishes, like exempting tips from taxes, it did little to address the broader affordability problem

Gidursky told me that the administration’s most acute problem was that gas prices, interest rates, and health insurance premiums kept getting more expensive, and the administration simply didn’t manage to address that. “Life is too expensive,” right-wing commentator Benny Johnson posted on X . “Especially for young people

Communists will win on the ‘affordability’ question if we don’t end the war and fix prices.” Still, coming up with an agenda that can actually address those voter concerns is more challenging, especially with the deficits and inflation concerns potentially constraining both parties from considering major new tax cuts and benefits

And making major long-term headway on spending cuts would likely require looking at programs like Medicare and Social Security that voters punished Republicans in the past for trying to remake, and that Trump moved the GOP away from considering touching
This tension between offering voters more direct help or retreating to austerity is likely to loom over the 2028 presidential campaign

But for now, Republicans are still struggling to figure out a clear agenda on the economy that resonates with voters.  “Voters are signaling they are unhappy with the economy, the Iran War, and corruption,” the influential right-wing activist Christopher Rufo posted . “It’s about policy.”

title: Democrats just seized one of the Republican Party’s most powerful weapons
excerpt: Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson. | Katina Zentz/San Antonio Express-News via Getty Images If you paid attention to Supreme Court litigation during t
body: Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson. | Katina Zentz/San Antonio Express-News via Getty Images If you paid attention to Supreme Court litigation during the Biden administration, you would have noticed a surprisingly high number of cases with names like Biden v

Texas’s outgoing attorney general, Ken Paxton, once bragged that he sued the Biden administration 106 times during his time as Texas’s top legal officer.  For years, Texas was the locus of the Republican Party’s quest to shape policy through litigation , especially during Democratic presidencies when Republicans could not use the US Department of Justice to bring cases
But the Republican Party’s entire legal strategy was dealt a very serious blow during Tuesday’s electoral landslide for Republicans
One of the casualties was Mayes Middleton, the Republican who hoped to succeed Paxton as attorney general
For the first time since the late 1990s , Texas’s top lawyer will be a Democrat, Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson
Texas’s central role in political litigation won’t end entirely, but this upset means no more lawsuits brought by the state of Texas that seek to impose the Republican Party’s policies from the bench

In the nearly three decades since a Democrat has served as Texas’s attorney general, Republicans have used their control over the state AG’s office to shape everything from immigration policy , to environmental regulation , to who receives overtime pay
But, thanks to Johnson’s victory this week, they will no longer control one of the most powerful litigation shops in the United States
Three reasons why Texas is so central to the Republican Party’s legal strategy The Texas attorney general role is such an important prize for Republicans for three reasons
One is simply that Texas is a big, wealthy state that employs many lawyers
The attorney general alone oversees nearly 750 attorneys , about as many as you may find in a large multinational law firm
So Texas can afford to divert several — or even several dozen — of these lawyers into partisan litigation

The second reason is that Texas’s federal courts are unusually friendly to Republicans, and they follow unusual rules that all-but-guarantee that the Republican Party will win short-term victories in many cases
Many of Texas’s federal trial courts effectively allow litigants to choose which judge will hear their case

That means that when Texas (or any other litigant challenging a Democratic policy) files a lawsuit, it can often handpick a judge who will embrace legal arguments that most judges would find ridiculous

In 2022, for example, anti-abortion activists selected Matthew Kacsmaryk , a Trump-appointed judge known for far right religious views and his reactionary views on sexuality, to hear their lawsuit seeking to ban the abortion drug mifepristone
Kacsmaryk promptly complied with their request — although his decision was eventually tossed out by a unanimous Supreme Court
The immediate upshot of Johnson’s victory is that the Texas AG’s office will soon be less relevant than it has been for many years

After being heard by a handpicked trial judge, moreover, federal cases in Texas appeal to the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, which is dominated by MAGA-aligned judges and is one of the few courts in America where the median judge is more sympathetic to Republicans than the median Supreme Court justice.  The Supreme Court, in fairness, often reverses this outlier appeals court
But the justices typically only grant about 60 of the 7,000 to 8,000 petitions asking them to review lower court decisions
So, once a Democratic litigant loses in the Fifth Circuit, their only recourse is to beg for mercy from a Republican Supreme Court that ignores most of the cases that are brought to its attention
And even when the Supreme Court does reverse the Fifth Circuit, it often delays that decision long enough to hand Republicans a significant policy victory
In 2021, for example, Kacsmaryk ordered the Biden administration to reinstate a Trump-era border policy
Though the Supreme Court eventually reversed Kacsmaryk, it sat on the case for nearly an entire year — leaving Kacsmaryk’s injunction in place the entire time

Similarly, after MAGA Judge Drew Tipton issued an unlawful order limiting the Biden administration’s authority over Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the Supreme Court allowed Tipton’s order to remain in effect for 11 months before finally intervening
Notably, both of these lawsuits were brought by Paxton, in his role as Texas attorney general

Of course, now that Texas will no longer bring the same mix of partisan cases to the Fifth Circuit, private litigants may still do so — the mifepristone case, after all, was filed by anti-abortion groups and by anti-abortion doctors, not by Paxton

But that brings us to the third reason why Republican control of the Texas attorney general’s office is so important to the party’s legal strategy: States are particularly effective plaintiffs in federal litigation

The Constitution only allows a plaintiff to bring a federal lawsuit if they can show that they were injured in some way by the defendant they are suing — a requirement known as “ standing .” This requirement often trips up litigants who wish to challenge a federal policy that they find objectionable, but that doesn’t actually impose any special obligations upon them
The mifepristone litigation fizzled, for example, because none of the plaintiffs could show that they were harmed in any way by the fact that mifepristone is legal
As the Supreme Court explained, “a plaintiff’s desire to make a drug less available for others does not establish standing to sue.” But the Supreme Court said in Massachusetts v
EPA (2007) that states are “entitled to special solicitude in our standing analysis,” so states are often allowed to bring suits that private litigants cannot
And a large state like Texas often has many expenses and revenue streams that are impacted by virtually any federal policy

In 2015, for example, the Fifth Circuit concluded that Texas had standing to challenge a major Obama-era immigration program because the program would allow more immigrants to reside in the state of Texas, and that would cost Texas money because it would have to issue these immigrants driver’s licenses
Of course, Texas is only one of three states within the Fifth Circuit
Once Johnson is sworn in as Texas’s Democratic attorney general, the Republican attorneys general of Louisiana and Mississippi will still be able to bring cases to this MAGAfied court
And they will enjoy the same “special solicitude” the courts give to Texas
But both the Mississippi and the Louisiana AG’s offices are much smaller than Texas’s
So they will likely only have the resources to bring a fraction of the number of partisan lawsuits filed by Paxton

The Texas AG’s office was also a major pipeline for talented Republicans to advance their careers No doubt because the Texas attorney general’s office played such an important role in shaping the Republican Party’s legal strategy, it was an attractive employer for many talented Republicans who spent a few years working in this office before moving on to bigger things

title: Abortion rights weren’t the story of the midterms. They still won.
excerpt: Mallory Schwarz (center), executive director of Abortion Action Missouri, celebrates the failure of Amendment 3 during the No on 3, Stop the Ban watch party in
body: Mallory Schwarz (center), executive director of Abortion Action Missouri, celebrates the failure of Amendment 3 during the No on 3, Stop the Ban watch party in St
Louis on November 3, 2026. | David Carson/St

Louis Post-Dispatch via Getty Images On Tuesday night, voters cast their ballots in favor of abortion access in Missouri, Nevada, and Virginia, reflecting the continued popularity of the issue across red, blue, and purple states, even as it fell out of the political conversation compared to other topics this cycle

All told, the abortion rights victories in this latest election will strengthen or preserve abortion protections for millions of women of reproductive age, as well as thousands of others traveling from more restrictive areas for care
With the latest results, there are now 14 states where voters have backed abortion rights in ballot referendums since Roe v
Abortion rights advocates saw their one big loss of the night in Idaho, where a citizen-led ballot initiative to challenge one of the nation’s strictest abortion bans failed
The measure aimed to legalize abortion up to the point of fetal viability (typically between 22 and 24 weeks of a pregnancy) and in medical emergencies

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints came out against the measure in September, while national reproductive rights groups largely avoided investing in the campaign.   “We will see more doctors leave the state as a result of this election,” Melanie Folwell, executive director of Idahoans United for Women and Families, said in a statement. “And, most urgently, women will continue to suffer needlessly under one of the most cruel abortion bans in the nation.”  The anti-abortion movement was not prepared to fight ballot measures that protected access in the 2022 midterm cycle, calling the five out of five losses they endured that night a “ wake-up call .” In the 2024 cycle, anti-abortion leaders spent more money and leveraged new tactics, including in Florida, where Republican Gov
Ron DeSantis actively attacked the proposed ballot measure to reverse the state’s near-total abortion ban

He directed his state agencies to threaten local TV stations with criminal penalties if they aired ads in support.  Still, seven out of 10 passed that year — and the latest results on Tuesday suggest there still is a significant group of voters who personally oppose abortion, or have reservations, but are unwilling to support sweeping bans and were comfortable with Roe v

The anti-abortion movement released statements acknowledging their “devastating” losses this cycle. “The pro-life movement must double down on our education and grassroots efforts so Americans can feel confident in rejecting abortion extremism, knowing women and the unborn are protected,” said Sarah Zagorski, a spokesperson from Americans United for Life.  Ballot measures have become a key tool for abortion rights advocates since the Supreme Court overturned Roe
Where they’ve won, activists have turned around and used those victories to go after restrictions still on the books

In Arizona, a 2024 ballot measure win set advocates up to strike down the state’s 15-week ban the next year, and a February 2026 ruling cleared the way for abortion pills by mail and telehealth and ended mandatory counseling, ultrasounds, and waiting periods
In Colorado, where voters in 2024 lifted a decades-old ban on public funding for abortion, lawmakers followed up by extending coverage to Medicaid recipients and public employees
But the ballot measure strategy has limits
In many states with abortion bans or early gestational limits, for example, citizens have no way to put a constitutional amendment on the ballot at all; only the legislature can
And of the ban states that do allow it, just two, Arkansas and Oklahoma, haven’t yet voted on abortion
Oklahoma organizers abandoned their effort in late 2022, and Arkansas’s was thrown out in 2024 over how signatures were gathered

Even a ballot measure win isn’t permanent: Missouri lawmakers forced a repeal vote this year on the amendment voters passed in 2024, and while that effort failed this week, it revealed how even state constitutional protections can be reopened
Ballot measures have restored access where the rules allow it, but to restore access for everyone, Congress will need to take action
Here’s a closer look at what happened last night
The abortion rights ballot measures and their results 1

Virginia: Question 1 The measure established a new constitutional amendment for a right to reproductive freedom, defined as “the ability to make and carry out decisions related to one’s own prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care, contraception, abortion care, miscarriage management and fertility care.” The state can still restrict abortion for women in their third trimester unless the fetus is deemed nonviable or a physician determines abortion is necessary to protect the life, mental health, or physical health of the mother

Know more : Abortion is already legal in Virginia through the second trimester, and third-trimester abortions currently require three physicians to approve an abortion, determining that continuing would “irremediably” harm the patient’s life or health
The new constitutional amendment will change that requirement to just one physician, which advocates say will help those who face emergencies in rural areas with fewer doctors
Certain life-threatening complications are only discovered, or only develop, later in a pregnancy
Opponents of Question 1 argued this change will reduce safety and have filed a lawsuit to challenge the amendment from being enforced
Activists say their new constitutional amendment will help ensure that Virginia stays a safe haven for access, even if the state turns back to Republican control in future years
Every Republican in Virginia’s legislature voted against putting Question 1 on the ballot
The number of abortions provided in Virginia increased by nearly 114 percent from 2020 to 2025 , partly because so many people living in the South now travel there for care. 2

Missouri: Amendment 3 The measure would have repealed the constitutional right to reproductive freedom that Missouri voters approved in 2024, and barred gender transition surgeries and puberty-blocking drugs for minors

The measure would have also prohibited abortion except in cases of “medical emergency, fetal anomaly, rape, or incest” and only allowed abortions in cases of rape or incest prior to 12 weeks of gestation
Know more: Missouri, which was the first state to completely ban abortion after Roe fell, became the first state in 2024 to overturn that ban
On Tuesday, voters rejected Missouri lawmakers’ attempt to overturn that repeal
The measure drew protest from some anti-abortion activists too, who argued that it didn’t go far enough because it stopped short of criminalizing pregnant women

Lawmakers also paired the abortion ban with a prohibition on gender-affirming care for minors, a new tactic for the movement, which in past cycles has argued that abortion rights amendments would let young girls transition without their parents’ consent. 3

Idaho: Proposition 1 This measure would have created a statutory right to reproductive freedom and privacy by establishing that the state can regulate abortion after the point of fetal viability, except in medical emergencies

The measure would have also clarified that the state can’t interfere with personal reproductive healthcare decisions, including childbirth, contraception, fertility treatment, miscarriage care, and abortion

Know more: National progressive groups did not invest as heavily in Idaho’s abortion rights ballot measure, with some groups like the ACLU reportedly steering clear because they did not think it went far enough to expand access. “ACLU national basically said, ‘We don’t like your policy

It’s not ambitious enough,’” the executive director of Idahoans United for Women and Families told the Spokesman-Review in September . (Asked for comment, Carolyn Ehrlich, the ACLU’s acting director of ballot measures, confirmed they did not back it. “Every campaign cycle, we carefully evaluate where the ACLU can make a meaningful difference,” she told me, adding that the group must “balance our vision for the future with our own limited resources and political analysis.”) In 2024, national groups including Planned Parenthood, the ACLU, and Reproductive Freedom for All also declined to invest in measures in Arkansas and South Dakota on grounds that the proposals did not go far enough.  In 2025, 850 abortions were provided to Idaho residents via “shield laws” from telehealth providers in other states, while more than 1,600 people traveled out of state to end their pregnancies

title: Five lessons from the blue tsunami
excerpt: US Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters during a midterm election night watch party on November 4, 2026, in Detroit. | Salwan Georges/Getty Images Welcom
body: US Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters during a midterm election night watch party on November 4, 2026, in Detroit. | Salwan Georges/Getty Images Welcome to The Midterms, Actually
Every week I’ll be writing about two things: one big idea or trend I see forming, and one thing I’m hearing from a voice on the ground
One big idea Tuesday night, in a midterm election for the ages, Democrats notched sweeping victories across the country
They took back both chambers of Congress, and possibly broke the spirit of a Republican Party that has been firmly in President Donald Trump’s grip for the last decade
Early race calls in Georgia and North Carolina
Surprise wins in Kansas, South Carolina, and (maybe) Mississippi? This was a bloodbath
And it was a vindication for pollsters who had been flagging signs of Republican underperformance all year

Most importantly, it was the clearest message the American public could send to Trump’s administration: This president, his priorities, and his war of choice in Iran are out of step with public opinion
Trump wasn’t on the ballot, but he repeatedly told people to vote like he was
Americans accepted the challenge and largely retired the GOP candidates functioning as his proxy
Thinking about our reporting on America, Actually , where we’ve been charting the path to America’s post-Trump future one episode at a time, here are five lessons I’m taking from the results
They apply to the coming legislative fights in Congress and to the 2028 presidential primary. 1
It really was a populist backlash Throughout the year, candidates from James Talarico to Abdul El-Sayed said this election wasn’t about right versus left, but top versus bottom
For two years, Republicans and their allies claimed Trump’s 2024 coalition was a firm realignment, a fundamental break from Democrats by working-class voters

Fast-forward to this week: The New York Times’ voter analysis shows every big demographic moved toward Democrats, including men (17-point swing, Latino voters (28-point swing), and Asian voters (17-point swing)
First, Trump flopped, breaking his promises to lower prices and avoid foreign conflicts, among other things
Second, Democrats refocused their message, especially after Zohran Mamdani’s 2025 mayoral win in New York City, on affordability and tangible economic concerns

That brought back voters they lost in 2024, and reinforced the multiracial coalition they needed to overcome Republican advantages: a GOP-leaning Senate map, heavily gerrymandered districts, and a massive spending edge driven by big donors

Issues that won: Affordability, anti-corruption, anti-data centers So how did Democrats drive the bottom-versus-top message? Universally, with affordability, and by highlighting the choices Republicans made to follow Trump into the political abyss
When we were at a Speedway in battleground state Pennsylvania, even Trump voters were frustrated with the price of gas
Everyone, and I mean everyone, could draw the line between the war in Iran and the cost at the pump
When Pennsylvania voters are talking about the Strait of Hormuz, that’s a problem
It’s also a clear sign the GOP plan to blame the 2026 economy on former President Joe Biden wasn’t working
Here’s what one voter said: “I blame the president because he indicated to us he’s gonna drop all these costs

I know it can’t happen overnight, but when is it gonna happen?… It’s outrageous.” Two other issues carried the populist mood: Corruption Democrats across the country began hammering Trump on corruption earlier this year, and there’s real evidence the message was potent
We heard it in Virginia, and candidates like Jon Ossoff and Talarico made it their calling card
It wasn’t just that Trump was for sale
It was that he and his family were profiting from big business while things got more unaffordable for you
Data centers The third ingredient in this populist stew
Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas, Senate candidate Annie Andrews in South Carolina, and House candidate Will Lawrence in Michigan made a data center moratorium central to their campaigns
Data center moratoriums went an astounding 43-1 when put directly in front of voters, a sign of just how unpopular the issue has become
And like affordability and corruption, the data center message was never about just one thing
Voters were mad about the secretive process
Anxious about what artificial intelligence means for the future of work
And particularly enraged that big technology seemed to be profiting at their expense

Issues that lost: The GOP culture war The GOP had a huge spending advantage this cycle, and so much of that money went into ads painting Democrats as extreme, particularly on social and cultural issues. “ Talafreako ” in Texas, who they portrayed as an effeminate vegan
The Hasan Piker obsession in Michigan and the openly anti-Muslim and bigoted ads and rhetoric there and in places like Minnesota as well
And repeated hammering of a tactic that worked for Trump in 2024: stoking panic about transgender rights or “biological males” in women’s sports
It flopped in 2026, and there’s no way around it
The spending spree didn’t just fail to pan out; they seem to have lit their money on fire, given how roundly Americans rejected the pitch

title: The Download: controlling AI agents and “Super Intelligence” loyalty tests
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules
While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want
Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal
Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions
But big questions remain about whether these mechanisms will work in practice

Here’s how reverse game theory could help make AI agents behave . —Amit Katwala Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order with just one directive: government agencies must rebrand artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” One month on, the rebrand is slowly appearing across government websites and documents, but it hasn’t caught on with everyone
Even some of the biggest names in tech still use “AI.” But the bigger concern is the new term becoming a political loyalty test: Those who use it signal allegiance to the administration
Those who don’t become targets for attacks
So one month in, who’s on board? —James O’Donnell This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter

One more thing The noise we make is hurting animals
Can we learn to shut up? As human society has expanded, animals have started struggling to hear one another
For many birds, the noise has grown so loud that they’ve begun to sing with faster trills
Now, their mating calls aren’t as effective.  The growing hubbub can also increase bird-on-bird conflict, and entire species that can’t handle urban clamor simply leave town for good
But there are technological solutions to the noises hurting animals—and they could help humans, too

title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
excerpt: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since
body: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991
But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare)

body: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country
